steps.text: To judge an attack on a castled king, **count at the weak square**: how many of your pieces attack it, and how many of his defend it, the king included. The weak square is usually part of the pawn cover, such as h2 or h7. More attackers than defenders is a reason to look further, not a proof.

steps.text: The count only helps if every counted piece really reaches the square: a piece standing in its way blocks a line and removes an attacker. steps.text: A king still in the centre is a target when lines can be opened toward him and his pieces cannot cover them in time. To attack him you need **open lines** and attackers that arrive first. steps.text: A direct attack is a commitment. After the first sacrifice you cannot take it back, and his replies are mostly forced. steps.text: The **Greek gift** is the bishop sacrifice on h7 (or h2). Bxh7+ Kxh7 drags the king out; then the knight checks from g5 and the queen joins on h5. It asks for a bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, a knight that can reach g5, and a queen (or another piece) that can join on h5. It is a pattern with conditions, not a trick that always works.

steps.caption: White to move. Only the black king defends h7, and the bishop on c1 guards g5.

line.say: The bishop takes h7 with check.
The king takes the bishop.

The queen joins. Two white pieces now attack h7 and one black piece defends it.
Black takes the knight with the queen.
The bishop takes the queen.

Along the engine's best-defence line White ends at least 2 points ahead.
The bishop on e4 attacks h7.
Only the king defends h7.
Once the knight has left f3 the queen on d1 attacks h5.

steps.text: Check these before you play it, as a **rule of thumb**: the bishop reaches h7 with check; a knight can check from g5 and no black piece can safely take it (a bishop on e7 can; a queen can if g5 is unguarded); a queen can join on h5; no black knight on f6 covers h7. If one is missing the sacrifice may lose a piece. The engine check decides.

title: How fast to attack: forcing now or calm first
outcomes: Chooses between forcing play now and a calm strengthening move, and gives the reason (king in the centre, or sound cover)
Explains why a calm move that adds an attacker is not passive
Tests whether a defender's piece already in place changes the right pace
Recognises a position with no attack to pace because material is simply free

steps.text:
How fast should an attack go? Two speeds.
**Quick:** forcing moves now (checks, captures, sacrifices), because the king is still in the centre or the defenders are not yet near.
**Moderate:** a calm move that brings one more piece to bear, because forcing moves would only trade your attackers away.
A calm move that adds an attacker is not passive.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's king is still on e1 and has not castled.

line.say: Check at once, while the king is still in the centre.
White takes the bishop with the queen.
The knight takes the queen.

claims.statement: Bxf2+ is the engine's best move.
Along the engine line Bxf2+ nets Black at least 4 points.
The white king is in the centre.
The calm Qd5 is far worse.

steps.text: **Moderate pace.** When the king is sheltered behind pawns, forcing moves often run out of pieces. A calm move that adds one more attacker can beat a check. Ask: which of my pieces is not yet attacking? This is a *rule of thumb*. Whether to attack at all is the lesson 'Count before you attack: attack now, not yet, or no'.

**Conditions.** Quick when the king is still in the centre or open files point at it. Moderate when the king is sheltered and you can add an attacker.
**Fails.** A slow move while the king can still castle gives him time. A calm plan fails when the defender's piece is already in place: test that before trusting the plan.

steps.text: A **pawn storm** pushes pawns at a castled king to open a file or diagonal for your pieces. It belongs mainly to **opposite-side castling**, where pawns are cheap and speed counts. steps.text: An attack needs **tangible superiority** at its target: more of your pieces bear on it than he can bring to defend it, and his own threats are not faster. So count: the pieces that attack the target, those that can join in a move, then his defenders. The count is a **rule of thumb**: it tells you where to look, and the move still has to be checked.

steps.text: **Calculating without moving pieces:** play the line in your head and look at the board only at the end. You need no photographic memory, only the list from the tracing lesson, kept current: *what moved, what is gone, what is attacked now.* Moving pieces while you think is a different skill; it hides whether you can hold the position. Six plies is a first target, a rule of thumb.

fxe5: the f-pawn takes the queen. Gone: the White queen. A black pawn now stands on e5.

Rxf7: rook takes rook. The rooks on f1 and f7 now face each other, and neither has a defender.

steps.text: **Write the list, with a reason for each.** The short list in your head becomes a paper list: two to four moves, **checks and captures first**, then **at least one quiet move** (no check, no capture). steps.text: Depth is a budget you split between lines, not one number for the whole position. Sort the candidates first. **Deep look:** a forcing line (checks, captures, threats) with few replies, and it keeps going. **Short look:** a move whose piece can be taken for nothing (it is loose), or a quiet move that starts nothing. **No calculation:** only one legal move. A rule of thumb, not a tested method.

steps.text: **When the sort fails.** It uses only what you can see: checks, captures, threats, and whether the moved piece can be taken free. A quiet move can hide the best line, so give quiet candidates a short look, not a pass. In an opening line you know, recall replaces calculation. Rule of thumb: stop deepening when the position is quiet or the result is forced, not when you are tired.

steps.text: A **tree** is a table you fill once. Rows are your candidates. For each, write the opponent's best replies (two is a start) and follow every branch about four plies to its end. A reply you never listed (the table looks complete and is not), and going back over a branch you already judged. In a quiet position few branches reach a verdict; a tree finds little. title: Track the line: what moved, what is gone, what is attacked
outcomes: Writes what moved, what left the board and what is attacked after a two-ply line, with no piece moved

Notices when a capture removes a defender or opens a line

steps.text: Calculating is not taking a mental photograph. It is **updating a short list** after every move: *what moved, what left the board, what is attacked now.* Start small: one candidate and one reply, so two plies, with the board in front of you and nothing moved. Then ask one question: **which piece is attacked now, and does anything defend it?**

steps.caption: Black to move. Follow the two moves without touching a piece, and update the list after each one. A piece is loose when it is attacked and nothing defends it.

line.say: Rxd2+: the d7 rook, which defended d8, leaves and takes White's rook with check.
Rxd2: White retakes. Black's rook is gone. White's d2 rook now faces the undefended d8 rook down an open file.

claims.statement: The rook on d7 defends the rook on d8.
Before the moves exactly one black piece defends d8.
After the two moves no black piece defends the rook on d8.
After the two moves one white piece attacks it.
Black's only loose piece is the rook on d8.
White has no loose piece.

steps.text: **Where tracking breaks.** A capture does two things: the capturing piece lands somewhere new, and the captured piece stops attacking and defending. A capture can also open a line behind it (a discovered attack). So ask again after every capture: *who defended what, and what is open now?* Two plies is a first size, a rule of thumb. Accuracy after the first capture matters more than length.

Tracking covers routes too. On paper, write every square a knight lands on when it travels from a1 to h8 on an empty board, then count. Counting by eye is where an extra move hides.

One smaller drill. You study a position for a few seconds, then some pieces vanish, and you tap the squares a piece can reach. It trains the same habit in a simpler form: remembering what stands where, including the pieces that block a line.

**Trace card: five minutes, away from the app.** Take a position from your own game or a book diagram. Choose one candidate and the reply you expect. On paper write three lines: *moved*, *gone*, *attacked now (defended?)*. Two plies only. Then set the position up and play the two moves to check. Mark each line right or wrong. The line that fails tells you what to watch next time.

title: Counter-attack or defend: count both races
outcomes: Counts how many moves each side needs and says whether to counter-attack or defend

steps.text: A **counter-attack** answers a threat with a bigger threat of your own. It works only if your own position survives the first reply and your threats arrive first. Count both races: how many moves does the opponent need, how many do you need, and are yours checks? A half-hearted mix of defending and attacking is often the weakest choice (a rule of thumb from the source idea, not a theorem).

steps.text:
A **fortress** is a set-up the stronger side cannot break, even when it is ahead. Here both sides have a bishop, on opposite colours, and White has one extra pawn, yet White cannot win.
In these examples the defender has a king beside the square the pawn needs next and a bishop with safe waiting moves. The tablebase confirms each example; it does not prove the same holds for other pawns or bishop colours.

steps.text: A defender has several resources: move the piece, defend it, block, capture the attacker, make a bigger threat, vacate a weak square before supporting it, give material back. **Vacate, then support** (a rule of thumb, not tested in this lesson). If your important piece stands on the weak square, move it off first, then support the square; supporting it while the piece stands there can leave both stuck.

steps.text: A castled king hides behind his **pawn cover**: the pawns in front of him, on his file and either side of it. A pawn that steps forward stops guarding the squares diagonally ahead of it. A **hole** is a square on your third to fifth rank that no pawn of yours attacks now or can attack later: an enemy piece can sit there and no pawn can chase it away.

steps.text: A hole matters when an enemy piece can reach it and your pieces cannot cover it, so a push is a warning sign, a **rule of thumb**, not a ban. steps.text:
When you are under attack, one **exchange** can do more than any quiet defensive move: it takes away the attacker's most dangerous piece.
Ask two questions. Which enemy piece is doing the damage? Which of my pieces can trade for it?
The rest of the lesson is about when this works and when it does not.

**What to check.** An exchange helps when it removes an attacker the opponent cannot easily replace. Before you trade, ask: is a second attacker ready to take its place?

**Rule of thumb:** fewer pieces usually help the defender, but only when the trade takes away the piece doing the damage.

steps.text: In **Trade off the piece doing the damage** you took away an attacker by exchanging. Now the harder question: is a trade the right answer at all? Under attack you can **trade** an attacker, **hold** by moving or guarding the target, or **counter-attack** with a bigger threat of your own. Start with the threat question: if I pass, what can he do? Then count his attackers.

**When a trade works.** It works when it removes an attacker he cannot replace. It fails when a second attacker is left: one exchange cannot answer two threats. **Rule of thumb:** count the attackers before you trade. A counter-attack is a third option only if your threat comes first and is bigger; no exercise here proves one.

title: Lucena: building the bridge

steps.text: **Lucena.** The pawn is on the seventh rank and your king stands in front of it, on the queening square, so the pawn cannot move. The enemy king is cut off: your rook holds a file it may not cross. If your king steps aside, the enemy rook starts checking. You win by moving the king out and sheltering it behind your own rook. It is a plan with conditions, not a reflex.

The king steps off the file.
Black's rook checks again, now along the e-file.
The king steps toward the rook.
Black checks along the d-file.
The king steps up the board, next to the fourth rank.
Black checks along the e-file again.
The rook blocks on e4 and the king defends it, so Black's rook cannot take it with a win. This shelter is the bridge.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Lucena needs a pawn on the seventh, your king in front of it and the enemy king cut off. Two moves often spoil it: promoting while the enemy rook can take the new queen, and blocking a check with a loose rook (one your king does not defend). The bridge is a block by your own rook, on a square your king defends. Before you count on the win, ask what else about the arrangement matters.

steps.text: A queen alone cannot finish the game: the lone king simply captures her. Checkmate with king and queen needs three things at once. The queen **gives check**. Every square next to the black king is **covered or occupied**. And the checking queen is **protected**, usually by your own king standing next to her. Look for all three before you move.

steps.text: **When it holds, and when it fails.** A queen check is mate only if the king cannot capture the queen and has no free square. The look-alike that fails: the same queen check with your king one step too far away. Before you play a check, ask: *what protects my queen?* Which corner the king sits in changes the route, not the method.

steps.text: The count is arithmetic. The halfmove clock counts half-moves since the last capture or pawn move, and at 100 either player may claim a draw. The tablebase tells how many more half-moves the win needs at best. **The win holds if the clock plus that number is at most 100.** First the sum: one move by each side adds two half-moves.

steps.prompt: White to move, bishop and knight against a lone king. The tablebase says the win needs 57 half-moves. The clock is 43 in the first position and 44 in the second; the third is the first reflected left to right. Predict each result.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb:** when the sum is close to 100, every move must be among the fastest. A move that looks as good can still cost the win. In the next two positions the clock leaves almost no spare time, so find the move that loses none. The third position is a different question: can the count be met at all?

No short method finds the fastest move. When the clock is high, prefer the move that keeps both pieces and the king together and cuts the king's escape squares, and check it with the tablebase after you answer.

steps.text: A winning side can throw the game away in one move. If the lone king is **not in check** and has **no legal move**, the game is a draw by stalemate, however much material you have. steps.text: **Count the king's moves after your move.** Check and a legal reply: play on. Check and no reply: checkmate. No check and no reply: stalemate. steps.text: A pawn race is a **counting problem**. Count each pawn's moves to the last rank: one move per rank, except that a pawn on its home rank may cover its first two ranks in one move. A king's distance to a square is the larger of the file gap and the rank gap. And ask **whose move it is**: the side to move spends its first move first. A pawn that arrives with no king in reach queens.

**When counting works**: both pawns are free to run and no king is near enough to interfere. **When it fails:** a king close to a pawn changes the count (the lesson *The rule of the square* shows how), and the first queen may be captured or checked at once. If the first queen has no check or capture, the other pawn queens one move later and the race may be only a draw.

steps.text: Can a lone king catch a runaway pawn? Count the pawn's steps to the eighth rank (for a black pawn, count towards the first rank) and draw a square with that many squares on a side, starting at the pawn. If the defending king is inside the square, or steps into it on his move, he catches the pawn. This **rule of the square** is a heuristic: it counts only the pawn and the defending king.

steps.text: **The square rule has limits.** (1) Your own king can escort the pawn, so a king inside the square may still lose. (2) A pawn on its second rank can move two squares, so draw the square from the square it will reach after the double step. Both are limits of a rule of thumb: the square counts only the pawn and the defending king, so check the position before you trust it.

steps.text: A queen usually beats a lone pawn. But when the pawn is one step from queening and its own king stands beside it, a **stalemate** trap can save it: a careless queen move leaves the weaker side with no legal move. The pawn's **file** decides whether the trap exists. Watch one trap first, then compare files.

steps.text: **When the draw works.** Take a pawn on the seventh, the weaker king on or next to the queening square, and the stronger king far away. Then the rook and bishop pawns (a, c, f, h files) can often hold by stalemate, while the knight and central pawns (b, d, e, g files) are lost for the pawn's side. 'Often' matters: the exact squares still decide, so the next positions are checked one by one. The nearer the stronger king, the less this holds.

title: Rook and pawn against rook: cut the king off

steps.text: A rook can **cut the enemy king off** along a file: the king may not step onto any square the rook attacks. A king cut off on the far side of the rook cannot stand in front of the pawn, so your king and pawn can advance while your rook keeps the cut. Which side of the rook the defending king is on decides the result.

**Pawn or position?** An extra pawn does not win a rook ending by itself (rule of thumb). Before a rook captures a pawn, ask whether the pawn is defended and what the rook gives up: a check, a file, the cut-off. steps.text: Two slogans: *always keep the rook active* and *never defend passively*. Both fail. The lesson *Active rooks: the pawn or the rook's position?* compared a capture with an active move. Now the defender must find the **only draw**: sometimes a passive rook move, sometimes an active one. Test the moves instead of trusting a slogan. **A tied rook** is one for which only a few moves hold. Here Black's rook cannot capture the pawn or check from the side: those moves lose. Rule of thumb: when the king is next to the pawn's file and the pawn is far advanced, the defender's rook may be tied to a rank. Move the king one file and the draw can vanish.

title: Rook endings: four habits and where they fail
outcomes: Puts the rook behind a passed pawn and predicts how the result changes when the rook stands in front of it
Checks which side of the rook's file the enemy king stands on, and predicts how the result changes when the king is not cut off
Predicts win or draw with the rook on the seventh rank, and names a position where the seventh rank is not enough
Finds the defender's far check instead of a close one, and spots a position with no passed pawn, where the rook-behind habit does not apply

steps.text:
Four rook-ending habits.
**Behind:** put the rook behind a passed pawn.
**Cut off:** keep the enemy king away along a file or rank.
**Seventh:** a rook on the seventh rank can shut the enemy king on the back rank.
**Distance:** the defender's rook checks from far away.
Each is a *rule of thumb* with exceptions. A **tablebase** (exact results for few pieces) checks every position.

steps.caption: White to move wins. The rook stands on e4, behind the passed pawn on e5. One line is shown.

line.say: The pawn advances. The rook on e4 defends it from behind along the open file.
Black's rook runs to the far end of the board.
The pawn reaches e7. The rook still defends it from behind, across more squares.
Black's rook takes the square in front of the pawn.
White's king steps up the board towards the pawn.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.
1.e6 keeps the win.
The pawn on e5 is passed.
White's rook is on e4.
After e6 the rook defends the pawn.
After e7 the rook still defends the pawn.

steps.text: **Why behind?** From behind, the rook defends the pawn along the file after every push, and each push gives the rook more open squares behind the pawn. In front of the pawn it blocks the pawn's path and loses a square with each push. This is a *rule of thumb*: some positions need a passive rook instead. First test the habit: predict each position, then check.

steps.title: Behind or in front?
steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook is behind its passed pawn. In the second it stands on g7, in front of the pawn; in the third Black's rook is on c6. Predict both, then check.

steps.text: **Cut off, and when it fails.** A rook on a file keeps the enemy king on the far side of that file, away from your pawn. If the king is already on the pawn's side of the file, there is nothing to cut off, and the win can vanish. A *rule of thumb*: check which side of the rook's file the king stands on, then predict.

steps.title: Is the king cut off?
steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook on e1 keeps Black's king on the far side of the e-file from the pawn. In the second the king stands on c7, on the pawn's side; in the third Black's rook is on b8, not a8. Predict both, then check.

steps.text:
**Seventh rank:** a rook there attacks the whole rank if it is open, keeping the enemy king on the back rank. It is strongest with an advanced passed pawn, but no guarantee.
**Distance:** the defender's rook checks from far away, where the king cannot attack it. A check right next to the king can simply lose the rook.
Both are *rules of thumb*. Predict, then check.

steps.title: The rook on the seventh rank
steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook is on the seventh rank and Black's king is shut in on a8. In the second Black's king stands on a6; in the third White's king is on e3, not d3. Predict both, then check.

steps.text: Pawns on the a- and h-files are special. A rook pawn has only one neighbouring file, so the attacking king can come at it from one side only, and the defending king can wait in the corner in front of it. Watch what a king in the corner can do, then predict.

steps.text: **How close is close enough?** With White's king on b6 and the pawn on a5, Black's king draws from squares close to the corner and loses from farther away. How close depends on White's king too. *Rule of thumb:* count Black's king moves to the corner. Predict, then check.

title: The rule of the square: the exact count
outcomes: Counts the pawn's moves to queen (with the double step from the second rank) and the defending king's steps to the queening square

steps.text: In **The rule of the square: can the king catch the pawn?** you drew a square. Now count. n: the pawn's moves to queen (from the second rank use the double step: b2 and b3 give 5). k: the king's steps to the queening square (the bigger of the file gap and the rank gap). King to move: he stops the pawn if k is at most n + 1; pawn to move: if k is at most n.

steps.text: **The extra step, and when the count holds.** The extra step is the new queen: a king beside it takes it. The count uses only the pawn and the defending king, so it holds when the pawn's own king is far away (*rule of thumb*; the tablebase checks every position here). It fails when that king is near the pawn or near the queening square: he can escort the pawn or guard the new queen. The double step adds nothing: b2 and b3 both give 5.

title: The tablebase lab: test a claim, do not just quote it
outcomes: States what a tablebase result is (exact for the side to move, seven pieces or fewer) and what it does not say
Decides whether a position can be looked up at all
Tests a conjecture with a position where it should hold and one where it should fail, predicting each result first

steps.text:
A **tablebase** stores every position with few pieces (seven or fewer, kings included) and its exact result under the usual rules for the side to move: win, draw or loss with best play. It is not an engine's opinion.
It gives the result, not the reason. This app has no tablebase tool, so the lab here is a paper-and-browser routine using any online tablebase.

The lab routine:
**1.** Write the conjecture as one sentence, with its conditions.
**2.** Write two positions that differ by one feature: one where it should hold, one where it should fail.
**3.** Predict both results before you look.
**4.** Query the tablebase.
**5.** Record the result and a reason a person could check by hand.
One failure refutes a conjecture. Many successes do not prove it.

steps.title: When can the lab answer?
steps.prompt: A seven-piece rook ending, the same ending with one more pawn, and an opening position. For each, decide whether a tablebase can answer, then check.

steps.text:
Conditions. A tablebase answers only for seven pieces or fewer. It names a result and never a reason, so 'win' needs your own checkable explanation before you teach it to anyone.
Rule of thumb: if you cannot state a reason another person could check, you hold a fact, not an understanding.

steps.prompt: Run steps 1 to 3 of the lab now on a claim from a book, a video or your own games (seven pieces or fewer). Save the note, then do the lookup later in any online tablebase and write the result and a reason beside it on paper; the app cannot reopen a saved note.

title: Spare moves: mutual zugzwang and the catch in the count
outcomes: Predicts the result of a locked pawn ending from the count of free squares and checks it against the tablebase

steps.text: The lesson *Spare moves: who runs out first?* counted free squares between two h-pawns. Now look at the same position with **either** side to move. In a **mutual zugzwang** whoever has the move is worse off. Predict first, then check: the tablebase gives the exact result. Start with White to move.

**Count, then check.** With no free square between the pawns, the side to move loses here. With one free square, the side to move wins. Rule of thumb: an even number of free squares means the mover gives way, an odd number means the mover wins. It holds only while both kings are tied to their squares and no pawn can still double-step. Change any of that and recount, or look the position up in the tablebase.

steps.text: **The catch.** A pawn on its starting square may move one square or two. That is an extra choice, and it can change who runs out of moves first. Before you count free squares, look at each pawn's square. In the next positions the plain count may mislead you: predict, then check.

title: Two knights cannot mate alone, but a pawn can change that
outcomes: Says that two knights cannot force mate against a bare king
Explains that a defender's pawn gives the defender spare moves, which can turn some two-knight positions into wins

steps.text: Two knights and a king look strong against a bare king. They are not: with best play they **cannot force checkmate**. Mate only appears if the defender helps. Test it before you read on: predict the result of the next position, then check.

**Result:** two knights against a bare king are a draw with best play. The knights can corner the king, but they cannot take away every square and still give check, so the defender can always avoid being forced into mate (or is stalemated). This position is checked by the tablebase. Now give the defender a pawn and see what changes.

**Why a pawn can help the knights:** a pawn that can still move gives the defender spare moves, so there is no stalemate. **Conditions:** bare king, draw. With a pawn on the board there are three outcomes: the knights can win (spare moves for the defender), the position can stay drawn (a blockaded pawn can leave the defender short of moves), or the pawn side can win by queening. Do not assume; classify each position.

title: Queen against rook: force the king away from its rook
outcomes: Finds the check that starts a forced win of the rook in a queen-against-rook position
Checks for a rook fork, a stalemating capture and an advanced pawn before playing a check
Predicts win or draw for queen against rook, including when the rook's side is to move

steps.text:
A queen is stronger than a rook, but it does not win by size alone. It wins by **forcing**: a check makes the king move, then one queen move attacks the king and the rook together (a fork), or the rook behind the king on the same line (a skewer).
In the positions below the rook falls. Your job: find the check that separates the rook from its king.

steps.caption: White to move. Look for a check that makes the black king stand in front of its rook.

line.say: Qa1+ is check along the first rank. Black must answer it.
The king steps to c2, onto the same rank as its rook on h2.
Qa2+ checks along the second rank. The king stands between the queen and the rook.
The king must leave the rank to escape the check.
Now the queen takes the rook.

claims.statement: White to move wins.
Qa1+ wins the rook along the engine's best defence.
After Qa1+ Kc2 the king stands on c2.
The rook stands on h2 on the same rank as the king.
After Qa2+ and Kd3 the queen attacks the rook on h2.

steps.text: A **tablebase** is a stored list of exact results for positions with few pieces. It gives the result with best play by both sides: win, draw or loss. It does not say how many moves a person needs, or how hard the defence is to find; that is not measured here. Read 'the queen wins' as a statement about perfect play, then practise the method until it is routine.

Check three things before a check.
**1. Who moves?** The rook's side to move may fork king and queen and draw.
**2. Stalemate.** Taking the rook can leave a lone king with no legal move: a draw.
**3. Pawns.** An advanced pawn can change the result; this method is for queen against rook alone.
Before each check, ask: can the rook then check and hit the queen?

steps.caption: White to move. The capture looks natural. Watch the black king after it.

line.say: Qxb1 wins the rook. Black's king on a8 now has no legal move.

steps.text:
In **Queen against rook: force the king away from its rook** you learned the method. Here you **play it out** against the tablebase, where every move costs. A tablebase gives the result with best play, not how many moves a person needs, so you set a move budget yourself.
The extra queen does not win by itself: the rook's side has one trick, shown next.

steps.caption: Black, the side with the rook, to move. The queen is stronger, yet this is a draw. Step through the one resource: a check that skewers king and queen.

line.say: Ra3+ is check along the third rank. The queen stands behind the king on that rank, so when the king steps off the rank, the rook attacks the queen (a skewer).
The king steps off the rank to c2. The rook now attacks the queen, but the king stands next to it. Any king move that is not next to d3 loses the queen.
The rook takes the queen.
The king takes the rook. Only the two kings are left.

claims.statement: Black to move draws.
After Ra3+ the position is still a draw.
After Ra3+ Kc2 Rxd3 the white king recaptures on d3.

steps.text: **Conditions.** The rook's side draws when it has the move and gives a check that hits the queen, directly or after the king steps aside, and the trade leaves only bare kings. That needs a king next to the capture square: the queen's king (previous board) or the rook's own. **When it fails:** no king covers that square, so the rook wins the queen free; or no check hits the queen, so the queen's side wins. Before each queen move, ask whether the rook has such a check.

steps.text: Now play against full-strength defence. **Plan before move one:** list the rook's checks, then pick a check that does not leave your queen where the rook can fork it. **Budget:** the move count shown is more than the tablebase's own distance to mate. title: Triangulation: a king detour that passes the move
outcomes: Explains triangulation: a king walk around three squares costs an odd number of moves and hands the move to the opponent

steps.text: Sometimes the winning position is on the board, but the wrong player is to move. A king can pass the move. Stepping out and back takes **two** moves, and the opponent can answer with a two-move shuffle. Walking round a triangle of three squares takes **three**. That is **triangulation**: your king ends where it started and the opponent has to move.

steps.caption: Black to move, and Black loses: its king has one legal move. The same placement with White to move is only a draw (Ka5, Kb5 and Kb6 all let the win slip). Triangulation tries to reach a placement like this with the other side to move.

line.say: Black's only legal move: the king goes to b8.
Kb6 is the only winning reply for White. Ka5 and Kb5 would draw.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result is a loss for Black.
The black king on a8 has exactly one legal move.
After Kb8 Black is still lost.

steps.text: **When it works.** The three squares must be free and safe, and the defender must have no triangle or waiting move of his own. If he has one, he answers in kind and the draw is back. Rule of thumb: ask first whether the position would win with the opponent to move; if it would and you are to move, look for a triangle. Opposition stays the first tool.

title: Zugzwang: when having the move is a burden

steps.text: **Zugzwang** means every move you have makes your position worse; you would rather pass. In some blocked pawn endings both sides are in zugzwang, so whoever has to move loses. Then the fight is about the move itself: the winner tries to reach that position with the other side to move.

Black's pawn is free to run.
White's king heads for the corner.
Black's king keeps close to the pawn.

claims.statement: With White to move, White loses.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Mutual zugzwang needs blocked pawns and no spare moves: only the kings can move. Then the side to move loses. It is a heuristic about such positions, not a law: when a king stands one step away, or has a detour that loses a move (**triangulation**), the move can be won back. Predict what changes.

steps.text: **Paris, 1858.** Paul Morphy has White. Black's moves are chosen together by two amateurs, the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard. Accounts say they played in a theatre box during an opera, and differ on which opera. The moves match two sources. Watch the first eight moves, then predict four White moves and judge one position that is not from the game. Before each, ask: which pieces are in the fight on each side, and which are still at home?

steps.text: **What the game used.** **Counting attackers and defenders**: the bishop on e4 had two defenders, then one, then none. **Overloaded defender**: after 22.g3 the queen on e2 defended both e4 and h2. **Removing a defender**: 22...Rxc3 took the knight. **Deflection**: 23...Rd2 attacked the queen, so taking the rook left e4 undefended. At depth 16 the engine rated Black over 2.5 pawns ahead before 20...Ng4 and over 10 ahead after 23.gxh4.

steps.text: **Botvinnik (White) against Tal (Black)**, game 6 of the 1960 world championship match, Moscow, 26 March 1960; Tal won. The opening was a King's Indian with White's bishop on g2. You play Black at three moments and White at two, each before seeing the game move, and compare your move with the engine's first choice and with the game. Engine numbers are a rating at a stated depth, not proof.

The queen moves to b4, still facing b2.

White's rook goes to b1, facing the queen.

title: Which squares does a piece attack?
outcomes: Taps every square a rook, bishop, knight or pawn attacks when other pieces stand in the way
Stops a line at the first piece it meets and keeps the squares behind it out
Knows a pawn attacks diagonally ahead, even when blocked, and not straight ahead
Says a defended piece is still attacked

steps.text:
A piece **attacks** a square when it could capture an enemy piece standing there (a pinned piece is covered in the check card below). If the square holds a piece of its own side, we say the piece **defends** it.
An attacked square need not hold anything yet. And the squares a piece attacks are not always the squares it moves to.

steps.caption: White to move. The lit squares are the squares the rook on e3 attacks.

line.say: The rook can take the pawn on e7. It is the first piece on the file; e8 behind it was never attacked.

claims.statement: These twelve squares are exactly the rook's attacked squares.
A black pawn stands on e7.
The rook can capture the pawn on e7.

steps.text:
Check before you trust 'attacks'.
**Lines:** a rook, bishop or queen attacks up to and including the first piece it meets; squares behind it are not attacked.
**Pawns:** the squares diagonally ahead (one square on an edge file), even when blocked; never straight ahead.
**Pinned pieces** still attack their squares (an enemy king may not step there), though they may be unable to capture. A defended piece is still attacked.

steps.prompt: White's d4 pawn and a black knight. Predict, then check.
Which rule did you reach for last: the line stops at the first piece, or the pawn attacks diagonally? Which one would you check first next time?

title: The board and its square names
outcomes: Names any square from its file and rank
Finds a named square on the board, from White's side or Black's
Reads a simple written move such as Nf3 or Bc4 and plays it

steps.text: A chessboard has 64 squares. The columns are called **files** and are named with the letters **a** to **h**, left to right as White sees the board. The rows are called **ranks** and are numbered **1** to **8**, starting at White's side. Every square has a name: its file letter, then its rank number. The white king starts on **e1**.

steps.caption: Watch the white pawn travel from e2 to e4. Every square keeps its name.

line.say: The pawn on e2 moves to e4.
Black's pawn on e7 moves to e5.

steps.text: To write a move down, use the piece's letter and the square it goes to: **K** king, **Q** queen, **R** rook, **B** bishop, **N** knight. Pawns have no letter, so a pawn move is just the square: **e4**. A capture adds an **x**: **Nxe5** means the knight captures on e5.

steps.title: Same board, other side
steps.prompt: Predict first: we turn the board around so you see it from Black's side. Does the name of the rook's square change?
How sure are you that you can name any square quickly, without counting? (low / medium / high)

title: Naming squares fast, from either side
outcomes: Names a square pointed at on either side of the board without counting from the edge
Uses the square colour as a quick check on a name
Does not mirror squares when the board is turned

steps.text: In **The board and its square names** you learned that a square is its file letter, then its rank number. Now the aim is speed. Two habits replace counting. First, read the letter and number along the board's edge. Second, check the **colour**: a1 is dark, and a square is dark when its letter's place in the alphabet plus its rank number is even (a=1, b=2). This holds on every square.

steps.caption: The bishop on a1 reaches only dark squares: b2, c3, d4, e5, f6, g7, h8. Check: d is the 4th letter and the rank is 4, 4+4=8, even.

line.say: The bishop slides to d4. It stays on dark squares: 4+4=8 is even.

steps.text: A real board has no letters on it, and this app's board turns to Black's side. The names stay with the squares, so only the picture changes. The common slip is to **mirror**: reading the square on screen as if White were looking, so b3 becomes g6. As a **rule of thumb**, find the letter on the edge first, then the number, and never copy the picture.

steps.title: One square, three ways of reading it
steps.prompt: The same white rook seen from White's side, seen from Black's side, and read by copying the picture as if White were looking. Predict first: which readings name the rook's square correctly?

steps.text: Limits of these checks. The colour test tells you a name is wrong, not which name is right: two dark squares both pass. The edge-letter habit needs letters on the board; on a real board learn the corners instead: a1 is dark at White's left, h1 is light at White's right (8+1=9 is odd). Both are **rules of thumb** for speed, so keep practising until naming is automatic.

steps.prompt: How sure are you that you can name any square pointed at, from either side, without counting? Which kind (a far corner, Black's side, a crowded middle) was slowest? (low / medium / high)

title: Taking pieces: is the capture safe?
outcomes: Finds a capture that wins an undefended piece
Checks whether the target is defended before taking
Knows that a capture is never forced and that a king cannot be captured

steps.text: You **capture** by moving onto an enemy piece and taking it off the board. A piece is **attacked** when the enemy could capture it next move. Captures are never forced, and a king is never captured: it is checkmated. Look at the target first. (The exact counting values come in the next lesson. For now: a queen has a higher counting value than a rook, bishop or knight, and each of those has a higher counting value than a pawn. "Points" means these counting values.)

steps.caption: The bishop takes a knight that nothing defends. Black cannot take back, so White has simply won a piece.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight on e5.
Black has no piece that can take the bishop back.

steps.text: Before you take, ask: **is the piece defended?** A piece is defended when a friend could take back on that square. If it is not defended, it is a *loose* piece and the capture is free. If it is defended, you may lose the piece you capture with, so compare what you win with what you can lose back.

steps.title: Same capture, one change
steps.prompt: The queen on d4 could take the knight on b6. Predict first, then check. In the second position a pawn defends the knight; in the third a pawn stands nearby but defends nothing.

steps.text: **When it holds.** A capture is free when the target is loose. It can also pay when the target is worth more than the piece you may lose (*rule of thumb*; the next lesson counts the points). **When it fails.** A defended target taken with a more valuable piece loses material. You may always decline, and a nearby piece that cannot capture on the square does not defend it.

steps.prompt: Before answering each 'take it or not' question: what did you check first, and in what order?

title: Free or defended: who can really recapture?
outcomes: Counts only the pieces that can capture on a square as its defenders
Decides whether a capture is free, wins points or loses points
Does not treat a nearby enemy piece as a defender

steps.text: In **Taking pieces: is the capture safe?** you learned to ask whether a piece is guarded. Now look closer. A piece is **loose** when it is attacked and nothing defends it. A defender counts only if it can capture on that very square with its own kind of move. A piece standing right next to the target proves nothing; count the pieces that actually attack the square.

steps.caption: The rook attacks the bishop on g5. The pawn on h6 defends it. The pawn on g6 stands in front of it but cannot capture on g5.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop for 3 points.
The h6 pawn recaptures. The g6 pawn could not have. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.text: So there are two questions. Is the square defended, by a piece that really attacks it? If it is, compare what you take with what you could lose. As a **rule of thumb**, with the counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9, a cheaper piece capturing a defended piece can still win points, and a dearer piece capturing a defended pawn loses them. The values are only a guide.

steps.title: Same capture, the defender changes
steps.prompt: Predict first: is the capture good when no piece defends the pawn, when a bishop defends it, and when a bishop stands nearby but cannot capture on that square?

Which kind of nearby piece fooled you most often: a piece of the wrong colour square, a pawn straight in front, or a rook behind a blocker? Name one square where you counted a defender that was not one.

title: Castling, and when you cannot
outcomes: Castles kingside and queenside
Knows the four conditions and which attacked squares matter
Spots when castling is not available

steps.text: **Castling** is the one move where two pieces move at once. The king goes two squares toward a rook, and that rook jumps over to the king's other side. It tucks the king away and brings a rook into the game. You can castle toward the h-file (kingside) or toward the a-file (queenside).

steps.caption: White castles kingside: the king goes to g1 and the rook to f1. Black castles queenside.

line.say: The king goes to g1 and the rook jumps to f1.
Black castles the other way: king to c8, rook to d8.

steps.text: You may castle only if: the king and that rook have never moved; every square between them is empty; the king is not in check; and the king does not pass over or land on an attacked square. The rook's own path does not have to be safe.

steps.title: Same castle, a rook arrives
steps.prompt: A black rook lands on f3. Predict first: can White still castle kingside?
Which castling condition would you check last in a real game: moved pieces, empty squares, check, or attacked squares?

title: Can I castle right now?
outcomes: Goes through the castling conditions in order and names the one that stops castling
Knows an attacked rook, or an attacked b-square, does not stop castling
Looks only at the squares the king crosses and lands on for attacks

steps.text: In **Castling, and when you cannot** you met the conditions. Use them as a checklist in this order: has the king or that rook moved (the right is gone for good)? Is any piece between them? Is the king in check now? Is a square the king crosses or lands on attacked? As a **rule of thumb**, go from the cheapest question to the dearest and stop at the first no.

steps.caption: A black rook attacks b1, yet White can castle queenside: the king uses only e1, d1 and c1.

line.say: The king goes to c1 and the rook to d1, although b1 is attacked.

steps.text: Only the king's own path matters. Kingside that is e1, f1, g1; queenside it is e1, d1, c1. An attacked **rook** does not stop castling, and neither does an attacked square beside the queenside rook (b1). But an attacked f1 or d1 does, even if the king would land on a safe square. A lost right never comes back, even if the piece returns.

steps.title: A rook is attacked, then a path square, then nothing relevant
steps.prompt: Black's rook can stand on h8 or f8, or a knight can stand on a8. Predict first: in which of the three can White castle kingside?
Before each answer, which question of the checklist did you ask first? Which one did you skip, and did skipping it ever give a wrong answer?

title: Check and checkmate: the three ways out
outcomes: Gets out of check by moving the king, blocking, or capturing the checking piece
Says 'checkmate' when none of the three ways exists
Knows a knight's check cannot be blocked

steps.text: When your king is attacked it is in **check**. You must fix it at once, in one of three ways: **move** the king, **block** the attack with a piece, or **capture** the piece that gives check. You may never make a move that leaves your own king in check.

steps.caption: White is in check. The king can step away, the bishop can block, or the rook can capture.

steps.text: Not every way is always open. A **knight** attacks by jumping, so there is no line to block. If the king has no safe square, nothing can capture the checker and nothing can block, it is **checkmate**: the game ends and the player in check loses. Test all three ways before you say mate.

steps.caption: The rook checks along the back rank (the row where the pieces start). The king's own pawns take away three squares, the rook covers the other two, and nothing can block or capture. Checkmate.

steps.text: **When it holds.** Check is answered by a king move, a block or a capture, never by ignoring it. Blocking works only against a line (rook, bishop, queen) with a square between; a knight check or a pawn check cannot be blocked. A double check cannot be fixed by one block or one capture, but you meet that later. *Rule of thumb:* list all three ways before you move; do not assume the king can step away, and do not assume a block exists.

steps.title: One pawn, opposite results
steps.prompt: Same rook check on the back rank. In one position the black pawn stands on f7; in the other it is missing. Predict first: which is checkmate? (The answer list also offers "stalemate", the next lesson; neither position is one.)
In the last questions you were not told what to look for. How sure were you of each answer? (low / medium / high)

title: Check, checkmate or neither?
outcomes: Says for each position whether the side to move is in check, checkmate or neither
Closes the three ways out in order before calling checkmate
Does not call a blocked line a check

steps.text: In **Check and checkmate: the three ways out** you found the way out of check. Now classify any position fast. First ask: is the king attacked right now? If not, it is **neither**. If it is, look for the three ways out: capture the checking piece, block the line, move the king. A knight check cannot be blocked. No way out at all is **checkmate**; any way out means only check.

steps.caption: The queen checks along h5-e8. Black has exactly one legal move: a pawn blocks on g6.

line.say: The pawn blocks the queen's line. Blocking is one of the three ways out.

steps.text: The order matters. First find the checker: a line with a piece in the way is not an attack, so an enemy rook behind a pawn gives no check. Pawn and knight checks cannot be blocked. Then ask: can it be captured? can it be blocked? Last, count the king's free squares. Checkmate needs all three closed at once: one free capture, block or square makes it only check. This is a rule of thumb for speed.

steps.title: One pawn changes the answer
steps.prompt: The rook checks along the back rank. Predict first: checkmate, check or neither with the pawns as shown, with one pawn moved, and with a far-away bishop added?

title: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting
outcomes: Spots loose pieces (attacked and not defended) on either side
Counts attackers and defenders of a square
Decides whether to start captures on a square by adding up the swaps, cheapest piece first

steps.text: A piece is **attacked** when an enemy piece could capture it. It is **defended** when a friendly piece could take back on that square. A piece that is attacked and **not defended** is **loose** (also called **hanging**): it can be taken for free. Spotting loose pieces, yours and theirs, is the first safety habit.

steps.caption: The queen attacks the pawn on b6 and the bishop on d5. Only one of them is loose.

steps.text: When several pieces fight over one square, count. List the attackers and the defenders. Start captures with your cheapest attacker. Add up what each side takes and gives, and stop when the next swap would lose more than it wins. More attackers than defenders is not always enough.

steps.caption: Two attackers, one defender, and the pawn goes first. Count the swaps.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight: +3.
The pawn takes the pawn: -1.
The bishop takes the pawn: +1.

title: Sorting endings: won, drawn or play on
outcomes: Tells a position drawn at once for lack of material from one that is only drawn with best play
Recognises endings that look drawn but are won, such as king, bishop and knight against a king
Sorts a mixed ending into won, drawn now or play on

steps.text: **Ways a game is drawn** listed the ways a game ends drawn. This lesson sorts endings by material. There are three boxes. **Drawn now:** no sequence of legal moves can reach mate, so the game ends by rule. **Won:** the stronger side can force mate. **Play on:** mate is possible, but nobody can force it. Ask the questions in that order.

steps.caption: King and one bishop against a bare king.

claims.statement: With best play the position is a draw (tablebase).

steps.text: **What decides the box.** Pieces that cannot mate, like one bishop or one knight, give a draw at once. Bishops that all stay on one colour cannot mate either, but only when no knights, rooks, queens or pawns are on the board. But king, bishop and knight against a king is a **win**, and two knights against a king is not forced, yet not drawn by rule. Counting pieces is a **rule of thumb**: check colours and pawns.

title: Is en passant possible right now?
outcomes: Decides from the last move alone whether en passant is possible
Lists a pawn's moves including the en passant capture
Does not allow en passant for a pawn that arrived earlier or by single steps

steps.text: In **En passant: capture a pawn in passing** you captured en passant when told to. Now decide for yourself whether it is possible. Ask: did an enemy pawn just move two squares in its last move? Did it land right beside my pawn? If both are yes, my pawn may capture it, landing on the square it jumped over. Only the last move counts: the game before that does not.

steps.caption: Black jumps two squares and lands beside the pawn on d5. White may take it as if it had moved one square.

White captures en passant: the pawn lands on c6 and the black pawn leaves c5.

steps.text: The **knight** moves in an L: two squares along a rank or a file, then one square to the side. It is the only piece that **jumps over** other pieces. steps.text: Rooks, bishops and queens need a clear path. A knight does not: it only needs a landing square that is not held by its own piece. That is why, at the start of a game, a knight can move while most other pieces cannot.

title: Checkmate in one: four patterns
outcomes: Finds a checkmate in one in the common patterns: back rank, queen next to the king, two rooks, queen with a bishop, knight
Checks every exit before calling a check checkmate

steps.text: **Checkmate** means the king is attacked and cannot escape: there is no safe square, nothing that can capture the attacker, and no way to block it. A **mate in one** does all of that with one move. A few shapes appear again and again. The first is the **back-rank mate**.

steps.caption: The rook checks along the back rank. The king's own pawns block its escape.

line.say: The rook slides to the eighth rank. It is checkmate.

steps.text: Before you call a check mate, check every exit: can the king step anywhere, can the checking piece be captured, can the check be blocked? A back-rank mate needs the king's own pawns to stand in front of it, with no square for the king to run to.

line.say: The king escapes to h7. It was check, not checkmate.

steps.text: Three more shapes. A **queen next to the king** is safe when your own king or another piece protects her. **Two rooks** can take turns: one holds a rank, the other gives check. A **knight's check** cannot be blocked, so it mates a king that has no square.

title: Is there a mate in one?
outcomes: Decides whether a mate in one exists in a mixed position, without being told
Lists the checks and tests each for king moves, capture and block
Says 'no mate' when every check has an answer

steps.text:
In **Checkmate in one: four patterns** you were told to look for a mate. Now nobody says whether one exists, and *no mate* is often the answer.

**Method.** 1) List every check you have: a move that is not a check cannot be mate. 2) Test each check on three escapes: the king moves, the checker is captured, the line is blocked. 3) If every check has an answer, say *no mate*.

steps.caption: Five checks, one mate. Test them one at a time.

line.say: Qc6 is the one check with no answer: the king's own pawns hold a7 and a5, and the queen covers the other squares.

steps.text:
*No mate* is a real answer. It is right when every check has an answer: a free square, a capture or a block.

**Rule of thumb:** if a mate looks easy but one defender stands next to the king, test again before you trust it. A piece that cannot reach the king's squares, the checking piece or the checking line does not change the answer.

title: Mates that need a closer look
outcomes: Finds a mate in one that uses a smothered king, a discovered or double check, or a promotion
Tests each check for king moves, capture and block before calling it mate
Rejects look-alikes that have a free square, a capture or a block

steps.text: In **Checkmate in one: four patterns** the mates were easy to see. Some need a closer look. First the **smothered mate**: a knight checks a king whose own pieces fill every neighbouring square. A knight's check cannot be blocked, so test two things: can the knight be captured, and does the king have a free square?

steps.caption: The king's own rook and pawns fill every square next to it.

line.say: Nc7 checks. Nothing captures the knight, and the king has no free square.

steps.text: **Discovered check:** a piece moves away and uncovers a check from the piece behind it. If the moving piece also checks, that is a **double check**, and only a king move answers it: capturing or blocking does not help. Test captures anyway: a knight that the king can simply take is no mate.

steps.caption: The knight stands on the bishop's diagonal.

line.say: Ng6 checks, and the bishop's diagonal is open too. Two checks; the king has no square.

steps.text: A **promotion** can be the checking move. The new piece decides whether it is mate, so test each choice: queen, rook, knight. A knight's check cannot be blocked and ignores pieces standing in the way, so a knight can mate where a queen does not.

steps.caption: The pawn can become a queen or a knight on f8.

line.say: The knight attacks h7 and nothing can take it. The king's own pieces fill g8, h8 and g7, and the white king covers g6 and h6.

steps.text:
These mates hold when, after the check, the king has no free square, the checker cannot be taken (for a double check, only a king move counts), and no piece can step in the way.

**Rule of thumb:** with a king boxed in by its own pieces, look first for a knight check, a discovered check or a promotion. It fails when one neighbouring square is open or a piece can interpose.

outcomes: Names the piece, the squares and any capture, check or castling in a written move

steps.text: A move record says **which piece** and **where it lands**. K king, Q queen, R rook, B bishop, N knight; a pawn move has no letter. **x** capture, **+** check, **#** checkmate, **O-O** castling kingside (**O-O-O** queenside), **=Q** a pawn becomes a queen. A number counts one White move and Black's reply: 1.e4 d5. Dots (1...d5) mark Black's move when a score starts with it.

steps.caption: A short score, played from the start. Read each record, then watch the move.

line.say: 1.e4: no letter, so a pawn moves, to e4.
1...d5: three dots mark a Black move shown alone. In a row it is written 1.e4 d5.
2.exd5: the e-pawn captures on d5. The x marks a capture.
2...Qxd5: the queen (Q) captures the pawn on d5.
3.Nc3: N is the knight; it lands on c3.
3...Qa5: no x, because nothing is captured on a5.
4.d4: a pawn move again, so there is no letter.
4...Nf6: Black's knight goes to f6.

claims.statement: 1.e4 is legal from the start.
A white pawn stands on e2 at the start.

steps.text: A record must name exactly one move. If two pieces of the same kind can reach the square, add the file the mover leaves from (**Nbd2**); if both stand on the same file, add the rank instead (**R1a3**). The marks **!** and **?** are a writer's opinion; they change nothing. The same record works for either colour and for a board turned around: square names do not change.

steps.title: Is the record enough?
steps.prompt: Two knights, one square, one change. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **Pawns** move straight forward, one square at a time, and never backward. From their starting square they may move two squares if both are empty. steps.text: Two details cause most pawn mistakes. The two-square jump is only for a pawn's first move, and only if both squares are empty. And a pawn captures diagonally, never straight ahead. Before moving a pawn ask: has it moved yet? And is the square ahead empty?

steps.text: The **bishop** moves in diagonals, as far as it likes, and cannot jump. A bishop stays on one colour of square for the whole game: one bishop travels on light squares, the other on dark squares. Captures work just like the rook's.

title: How the king moves
outcomes: Taps the squares a king can step to, never onto an attacked square or next to the enemy king

steps.text: The **king** moves one square in any direction. He is the piece you must never lose, so there is one extra rule: **a king may never move onto a square the enemy attacks** (a square where an enemy piece could capture).

steps.caption: The black rook attacks the whole fifth rank. The king cannot step onto it.

steps.text: Two kings can never stand on neighbouring squares either: each would attack the other's square. So the squares around the enemy king are off limits, even if no other piece attacks them.

The king can capture too, but only if the piece is not guarded. A piece is **guarded** (or defended) when a friendly piece could recapture on its square. **When it holds:** step to free or safely capturable squares. **When it fails:** an attacked square, a square next to the enemy king, or a guarded piece. Ask before you capture: which enemy pieces attack the square I am about to land on?

steps.text: A pawn that reaches the last rank is **promoted** as part of the same move: you choose a queen, rook, bishop or knight of your own colour, never a king or a pawn. You may have several queens. The pieces you already have do not limit the choice.

steps.text: A pawn promotes by moving straight ahead onto an empty last-rank square, or by capturing an enemy piece one step diagonally ahead. If a piece blocks the square ahead, look at both diagonals. A pawn cannot capture its own piece, and it must be on the seventh rank (the second, for Black) to promote on this move.

steps.text: The queen is usually the best choice, as a rule of thumb. title: How the queen moves
outcomes: Taps every square a queen can reach, stopping in front of its own pieces and on the first enemy piece

steps.text: The **queen** is the strongest piece. She moves like a rook and a bishop combined: any distance along a rank, a file or a diagonal. She cannot jump, and she captures the same way: by landing on an enemy piece. That gives her eight lines out of her square.

steps.caption: Eight directions. Two white pawns and two black pawns decide where each line stops.

steps.text: **When it holds:** the queen slides along any of her eight lines until something stops her. A friendly piece stops her one square early; an enemy piece can be captured, and she stops there. **When it fails:** she never moves like a knight, and she cannot jump over anything. Each line is blocked separately, so a blocker on one line leaves the other seven alone.

title: How the rook moves

steps.text: The **rook** moves in straight lines: along a rank (sideways) or a file (up and down), as far as it likes. It cannot jump over pieces. To **capture**, it lands on an enemy piece and takes it off the board. It can never land on a square holding its own piece.

steps.caption: The rook slides until something is in the way. It can take the black pawn on d7, but not go past it.

steps.text: Before you move a rook, ask three questions. Is the square on its rank or its file? Is anything standing between? Whose piece, if any, is on the square? Empty or enemy: allowed, and a captured piece ends the slide. Your own piece: not allowed. These are rules of the game, not rules of thumb, so they hold in every position.

steps.text: **En passant** means 'in passing'. When an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands right beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had moved only one square. Your pawn goes to the square the enemy pawn passed over, and the enemy pawn is removed. You must do it on the very next move, or the chance is gone.

steps.text: It works only on the move right after the two-square jump, and only for a pawn beside the jumper. If the enemy pawn arrived earlier, or by single steps, the right is gone; only the last move counts. Other pieces do not change the timing rule. (Like any move, the capture is not allowed if it would leave your own king in check; you meet that later.)

title: Stalemate: no move, but no check
outcomes: Says stalemate when the side to move has no legal move and is not in check
Tells checkmate from stalemate

steps.text: You know checkmate: the king is in check and has no way out. **Stalemate** is the lookalike: the player to move is **not** in check but has **no legal move at all**. The game is a **draw**, not a win for the side that moved last. One question separates them: is the king attacked right now?

steps.caption: Black to move. The king is not attacked, but every square it could use is covered by the queen or the white king. No legal move: stalemate, a draw.

steps.text: **When it holds.** Stalemate needs both facts: no check, and no legal move, for any piece. A king boxed in may still be free if another of its side's pieces can move. A big material lead does not prevent it: the stronger side is the one who must avoid it. *Rule of thumb:* before a quiet move near the enemy king, count its legal moves, and count the legal moves of its other pieces too.

steps.text: Before every move, ask two questions. **1. What does my opponent's last move threaten?** (a capture, a check, a checkmate). **2. Is any of my pieces loose?** (attacked, and not defended). title: Piece values: counting what you win and lose
outcomes: Says the counting value of each piece and which of two pieces is worth more
Adds up a capture and recapture to say whether a trade gains, loses or is even
Knows the values are a rule of thumb and that checkmate beats the count

steps.text: To compare trades, players give each piece a **counting value**: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king has no value because it is never traded; it is checkmated. The value belongs to the kind of piece, It does not depend on its colour, on the square it stands on, or on which piece takes it. These numbers are a *rule of thumb*, a first guide and not a law.

To judge a trade, **add what you take and subtract what you lose**. Taking a piece that is then taken back is a trade. A good trade gives you more points than it costs, even when you lose a piece. Pieces are not counted by number: a knight and a bishop for a rook is 6 for 5, so it gains a point although two pieces change hands for one.

steps.caption: A defended rook can still be worth taking with a knight. Add up the swap: what you take, minus what you lose.

line.say: The knight takes the rook: White gains 5.
The pawn takes the knight: White loses 3.

steps.title: Same trade, one change
steps.prompt: A rook on d5 is defended by a pawn. Predict first what the capture does to White's points. Then see what changes when the capturing piece changes, and when only the colours change.

steps.text: **When it holds.** The counting values compare trades when nothing else is happening. Take more than you give and you gain; equal values give an even trade. **When it fails.** The values do not see everything. Checkmate ends the game whatever the count says, and later you will meet pieces worth more or less than their usual points. Treat the count as a guide, not as proof.

steps.text: **What this lesson does and does not claim.** It gives a formula you can compute, and a few dates, each with its sources. **The Elo expected score.** According to Wikipedia's article on the Elo rating system, player A (rating R_A) against B (rating R_B) has expected score E_A = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B - R_A)/400)); a win counts 1, a draw 0.5. The FIDE Handbook (section 8.1.2) tabulates .64 for the higher-rated player at about 100 points difference and .76 at about 200. The formula gives 0.640 and 0.760: they agree there.

title: How the rules took shape: reading dates with care
outcomes: Names three rule changes (queen and bishop, stalemate, fifty-move rule) with each date's source, and whether one source or two give it

steps.text: **What this lesson does and does not claim.** It reports a few dates about the rules, each with its source. Where two sources I read agree, I say so; where only one gives a date, the card says so. It gives no stories, no quotes and no opinions on whether a rule is better. Historical claims cannot be checked by the engine, so you will practise asking: who says this, what do they actually show, and what is missing?

**The queen and bishop.** According to Wikipedia (History of chess), they stayed weak until between 1475 and 1500, when their modern moves started in Spain, in the Kingdom of Valencia. According to the Valencia Chess History Society, the poem *Scachs d'amor*, composed around 1475 in Valencia, is the earliest known text describing the modern rules. Neither source dates the bishop's change separately. Both are secondary sources. The sources I read give no shared date for castling or en passant, so none is given.

steps.text: **Stalemate: the old rule.** According to John McCrary (US Chess, 2021) and Edward Winter (chesshistory.com), Arthur Saul's 1614 book treated stalemate as a loss for the player who gives it. Pratt still defended that view in 1805 (McCrary) or 1806 (Winter): the sources differ by a year, so I give both.

**Stalemate: when it changed.** Winter alone gives about 1807 for clubs dropping the loss rule, and McCrary alone gives 1808 for English books proposing a draw. McCrary adds that it was a draw everywhere by the mid-1800s. Treat each of those dates as a lead, not a settled fact.

steps.prompt: Look at the two stalemate cards.

fields.label: Which statement there rests on only one source or on sources that differ?

steps.text: **The fifty-move rule.** Wikipedia and chessbio.com agree that FIDE abolished the longer-limit exceptions in 1992. Only Wikipedia gives 1561 (Ruy López) for the rule's introduction. A separate automatic 75-move draw also exists; the only date I found for it, 1 July 2014, comes from chessprogramming.org alone.

steps.prompt: Look at the fifty-move card.

steps.text: **How to read such claims.** A date from one source is a lead, not a fact. Two sources that copy each other count as one. 'Around' and 'between' mark real uncertainty, so keep them when you repeat a claim. Where sources disagree, say so. For further reading, the Library holds public-domain chess books from the 1800s and early 1900s; they are old sources, so read them as evidence of what was written then.

steps.text: **Answers.** A is a lead only: one site, nothing to compare. B counts as one source: Book Z copies Book Y, so agreement adds nothing. C is two sources, still secondary: they cite different origins and agree, which is stronger, but both are second-hand accounts and could still be wrong.

steps.text: In **Who is making the threats?** you listed threats and the replies they force. Now decide what to do with an initiative. The **safety scan** is the two questions from the threat lesson, run on every move in about ten seconds.
**1. What did my opponent's last move threaten or open?**

steps.text: Do not play the first good-looking move. Make a short **candidate list**: two to four moves, forcing moves first. Then follow each for about three **plies** (a ply is one move by one side): your move, the opponent's best reply, your next move. Drop candidates that clearly fail. Two to four is a habit to try, not a rule.

steps.text: To follow a line you must hold the board in your head. **Drill:** you study a position for 15 seconds, then some pieces vanish from the board. You must still say where a piece can go. This is a training exercise for seeing lines, not a chess rule.

**Short lines have limits.** Three plies are enough when every move is forcing. They can mislead when a sacrifice pays off later: a line that looks bad at ply three can be mate at ply five. And in quiet positions the candidates may not separate at all.
Ask: **is the last move of my line quiet or forcing?**

title: Cross out, then check from the other side
outcomes: Crosses out candidates one at a time with one concrete reply each
Checks the surviving move from the opponent's seat, in a different order from the one that found it
Finds a quiet refutation that a search of captures and checks misses

steps.text: Two steps, in this order. **Eliminate:** for each candidate, look for one concrete reply that refutes it: a capture, a check, a threat. Cross out what falls. **Verify:** for the survivor, change seats. In the position after your move, list the opponent's checks, captures and threats, then find his best reply. Do not re-walk your own line in the same order: it tends to repeat the same blind spot.

steps.caption: White to move. One candidate is crossed out in two moves.

line.say: Nxe8+ takes a rook with check. It looks strong.
The rook on f8 takes the knight, and nothing of White's defends it.

claims.statement: Nxe8+ is at least 300 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After Nxe8+ the knight on e8 is attacked by 2 black pieces.
After Nxe8+ the knight on e8 is loose.

steps.text: **Verifying is not recalculating.** You found the line from your side, so walking it again in the same order shows the same things. Switch sides and change the order: his checks first, then his captures, then his quiet threats. **Rule of thumb:** spend it where a mistake is costly and cannot be taken back. A position with one legal move has nothing to cross out.

**Some refutations are quiet.** A search of captures and checks crosses out the easy candidates. A candidate that survives that search may still fail to a quiet move: one that captures nothing and gives no check but makes a threat or traps a piece. That is why the survivor gets its own look from the other side. Next: find a quiet refutation.

**Test the escape squares before you trust a perpetual.** A run of checks forces a draw only if every reply Black has leads back into the same checks: no capture of the checker, no block, and no king step that gets out of them. List the king's squares first, then ask where each one leads. A free square often ends the checks, but not always.

steps.caption: White is far behind. Can the knight keep checking?

line.say: Ng6+. Nothing can take the knight, and the king has one square: h7.
Kh7 is forced.
Nf8+. Again nothing can take it, and the king's only square is h8.
Kh8 is forced. Ng6+ would now repeat the position after the first check.

claims.statement: After Ng6+ the black king on h8 has exactly one legal move.
After Ng6+ no black piece attacks the knight on g6.
After Ng6+ Kh7 Nf8+ the black king on h7 has exactly one legal move.
After Nf8+ no black piece attacks the knight on f8.

title: Caro-Kann Defense: the bishop outside, and three branches
outcomes: Names the Advance, Classical and Exchange branches by their move orders

steps.text:
**The Caro-Kann Defense** starts 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5. Black supports d5 with the c-pawn, so the bishop on c8 can still leave the pawns before ...e6 (compare the French, where ...e6 comes first).
Our opening data names three main branches: **Advance** (3.e5), **Classical** (3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5) and **Exchange** (3.exd5 cxd5). Pawn chains and breaks are taught elsewhere (the chain and breaks lessons); here we use them in one opening.

The pawn supports d5. The bishop is already outside it.
White brings out the last minor piece on the kingside. Think about what Black's c-pawn can do next.

claims.statement: 3.e5 is legal.
After 3.e5 the pawn on d4 is the base of a chain: it defends e5 and no pawn defends it.
After 4.Nf3 two white pieces defend d4 (queen and knight).

Third moves: 3.e5 in 5,097, 3.exd5 in 1,693, 3.Nc3 in 1,422, 3.Nd2 in 739, 3.f3 in 315. After 3.e5 the results were 1,975 White wins, 1,757 draws, 1,365 Black wins.

steps.text:
**When these ideas hold.** In the checked pair, ...c5 is the engine's top move after ...e6 and loses at least 80 centipawns before it (depth 16). In the Classical, after h4 the engine picks ...h6; ...Nf6, ...Nd7 and ...e6 lose at least 150.
**Question to ask:** has the supporting move been played? Here ...e6 comes before ...c5. Bringing the bishop out first is a choice that keeps its diagonal open, not a law. In the Exchange structure the c-pawn is gone, so ...c5 does not exist. Check the position first.
