title: The French Defence: chain, break and bad bishop
outcomes: Names the base and head of the French Advance chain and the lever that attacks the base
Counts the attackers and defenders of d4 before capturing or defending it
Says why Black's c8 bishop is the problem piece and where Black's counterplay comes from
Tells a position with the chain from one without it before choosing ...c5

steps.text: **The French Defence** starts 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 (ECO C00). After 3.e5, the *Advance Variation* (C02), White's pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain, and Black's pawns on e6 and d5 answer it. This lesson is about that one structure: where each side plays, and why. It assumes you know a chain's base and head (*Pawn chains: attack the base*) and why a bishop can be bad (*Good and bad pieces*).

steps.caption: A main line of the Advance Variation, step by step.

line.say: White takes space in the centre.
Black prepares ...d5. This is the French Defence (ECO C00).
White builds a pawn centre.
Black challenges it at once.
White advances. The pawns on d4 and e5 now form a chain: base d4, head e5. ECO C02, Advance Variation.
Black attacks the base with a pawn.
White supports the base with a pawn.
A second attacker joins: the knight.
A third defender joins: the knight.
The queen lines up behind the c5 pawn, aimed at d4 and at b2.
A quiet pawn move on the queenside.
Black closes the queenside. The pawns c4, d5 and e6 now form Black's own chain.

claims.statement: After 3.e5 the white pawn on e5 attacks f6, so a black knight on f6 could be captured.
After 3...c5 five of Black's eight pawns stand on light squares, the colour of the c8 bishop.
After 3...c5 a black pawn attacks d4.
After 5.Nf3 three white pieces defend d4 (pawn, queen, knight).
After 4...Nc6 two black pieces attack d4 (pawn c5, knight c6).
After 5...Qb6 the queen attacks b2.
After 6...c4 the pawn on d5 defends the pawn on c4.
After 6...c4 the pawn on e6 defends the pawn on d5.
After 6...c4 the engine (depth 16) rates the position within 0.6 pawns of level, from White's side.

steps.text: **What strong players chose.** In our master data (329,379 games from The Week in Chess and Lichess broadcasts, both players rated 2,500 or more, 2012 to 2026), 11,236 games reached 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5. White then played 3.Nc3 in 5,659, 3.Nd2 in 2,681, 3.e5 in 1,806 and 3.exd5 in 957. After 3.e5, Black chose 3...c5 in 1,751. These count games; none is an evaluation.

**White's plan.** The pawn on e5 attacks f6 and d6, so a black knight on f6 would be attacked by a pawn. In this line White usually keeps the base d4 defended with the pawn on c3, the knight on f3 and the queen along the d-file. Before any other idea, count the attackers and the defenders of d4.

**Black's plan.** Black's pawns on e6 and d5 stand on light squares, the colour of the c8 bishop, so that bishop is hemmed in. Black's counterplay is elsewhere: the lever ...c5 and then ...cxd4 hit the base, and bring the knight and the queen to bear on it. The bishop stays a problem until Black finds it a square or a trade; if ...c4 closes the queenside, it gets worse.

**When this holds.** *Rule of thumb:* in a chain, attack the base, not the head. It works here because a chain exists and d4 needs defenders against c5 and the knight. It does not apply when no chain stands: after 3.Nc3 or 3.exd5, ...c5 is rated at least 0.6 and 1 pawn worse at depth 16. And a bad bishop is bad *now*, not forever. Ask first: is there a chain, and who attacks and defends its base?

steps.text: **When the d4 break fits.** *Rule of thumb:* break in the centre when a pawn can recapture on d4. Here c3 does that, so after 5.d4 exd4 White chooses 6.cxd4 or 6.e5 (masters: 6.e5 in 534 games, 6.cxd4 in 219). Black's counter to 6.e5 is ...d5; after 6.cxd4 Bb4+ a check comes first. Without the c3 pawn, no pawn can recapture on d4. *Exception:* if one of your pieces is attacked, deal with that first, because a break does not answer the attack. You will meet this once, unlabeled, later.

steps.text: **The Najdorf Sicilian.** After 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3, Black plays **5...a6**. The opening data we ship names this position *Sicilian Defense: Najdorf Variation* (ECO B90). This lesson covers only what belongs to this opening: why the a-pawn moves, two pawn set-ups, and one plan for each side. Engine numbers are evidence at depth 16, not proof; game counts are results of games, not evaluations.

steps.text: **Two set-ups.** After 6.Be3, Black's two most common pawn moves in our master data are ...e5 and ...e6 (see the counts later). With **...e6** no black pawn attacks White's knight on d4 and the pawn on e6 guards d5. With **...e5** the pawn attacks that knight, and d5 becomes a square no black pawn can ever guard, because Black's c-pawn is gone. Study both boards, then tap White's outpost.

steps.text: **A plan belongs to a structure.** A move from one set-up can be a mistake in another. Two questions before you borrow a move: what does Black's last pawn move attack, and does my plan still make sense there? Next, a mistake for each colour. **When this holds.** *Rule of thumb:* the f3, Qd2 and g4 plan goes with ...e6, where no black pawn attacks the knight on d4. After ...e5 the knight must move first and d5 becomes the point of the structure. A plan fails when one feature changes, not when the opening name changes. Here that feature is one black pawn. title: Queen's Gambit Declined: the Exchange Variation and its plans
outcomes: Names the pawn structure that arises by move 7 in the Exchange Variation (White: d4 and e3 and no c-pawn; Black: c6 and d5 and no e-pawn) and the order of moves that reaches it
Starts the minority attack with b4 only after counting what attacks and defends the pawn, and checks what the opponent's last move attacks before carrying on with any plan
Chooses between two exchange offers for Black by checking them, not by the idea alone
Sees that a plan in the centre or on the kingside (Ne5, f4) can be as good as the minority attack, instead of treating one plan as the only one

steps.text: **Queen's Gambit Declined** (ECO D30): 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6. In our online data (4,752,291 games, September 2026) 63,292 games reach this position, and 6,259 reach the position named the *Exchange Variation*, after 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.cxd5. This lesson follows the Exchange Variation, where both sides have clear plans to test. Its pawn structure (White d4 and e3, Black c6 and d5, no e-pawn) is close to the one in the Carlsbad lesson, but not identical: here Black has no e-pawn.

steps.caption: Position after 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6, White to move. Step through one line of the Exchange Variation. Other moves are possible; this line shows how the structure arises.

Nf6 develops a knight and defends d5.

Black retakes with the e-pawn. White now has no c-pawn and Black has no e-pawn.
Bg5 attacks the knight on f6.
Be7 defends the knight on f6.
e3 supports the pawn on d4. White now has pawns on d4 and e3.
c6 supports the pawn on d5. Black now has pawns on c6 and d5.
Bd3 aims the bishop along the diagonal to h7.
Nbd7 develops the last knight and defends f6.

Black castles kingside. Both sides now have the pieces for the plans on the next steps.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results of games, not evaluations). Source: our masters data, 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. After 3.Nc3 Nf6, White played 4.cxd5 in 4,184 of 5,794 games (Bg5: 813, Nf3: 739). Of those 4,184 games White won 1,493, 1,700 were drawn and Black won 991. After 8...O-O, White played Nf3 in 53 games and Nge2 in 36. Samples are small; results also reflect the players.

**When the minority attack fits (rule of thumb).** White has two pawns against three on the a-, b- and c-files, the pawn pushed to b4 can be supported (here the rook on b1 defends it), and Black has no quicker threat. It does not fit when something of yours is attacked. Ask first: what did my opponent's last move attack? The next item shows what skipping that question costs.

**Black's side (rule of thumb).** Black often looks to exchange minor pieces, for example a knight against a bishop that has come to g5 or g3. Condition: the exchange must be safe in the position in front of you. In the next item two knight moves both attack the bishop, and the engine rates them very differently. Check the move, not just the idea.

title: An odd move: answer it or ignore it
outcomes: Sorts an odd move into one that attacks something and one that threatens nothing
Replies well when the odd move attacks a loose piece
Sees when an odd move is harmless and carries on with the opening habits

steps.text: **They left the book: three questions** gave you the questions with labels. Now there is no label, and the first job is a sorting job. Does the odd move attack something of yours, so that a piece is loose? Then answer it. Does it threaten nothing? Then your habits are free again. A quick test: *if I passed, what could they take?*

Not every odd move is a threat. An early queen move or an edge pawn can look alarming and threaten nothing at all. Treat 'harmless' as a claim to test, not a feeling. Pass in your head, then look at every capture and check the opponent would have: does any of them win material or give mate? If none does, the move is harmless. Even then, ask what the move gave up.

steps.title: Answer it or ignore it?
steps.prompt: Black's odd move attacks a loose piece in the first position. Predict whether the second odd move also needs an answer, then check.
When an opponent plays something you do not know, which do you do first: look for what it attacks, or look up what it is called? What would you change?

title: A trap after the book: calculate, then name the habit
outcomes: Calculates a reply when an odd move comes with a trap behind the natural reply
Says which opening habit the odd move broke
Tells a sacrifice that works from a look-alike that fails, by checking the position and not the pattern

steps.text: **An odd move: answer it or ignore it** sorted odd moves into threats and harmless ones. Some odd moves are neither: they invite your natural reply, and the natural reply is the mistake. When a capture or a developing move seems obvious right after an odd move, calculate it two moves deep before you play it. Ask what your move leaves loose and what it opens.

Now name the habit. In the position you just met, Black has moved the same knight three times (...Nf6, ...Ng4, ...Nxe5), brought the queen out and put a bishop on b4. Naming the habit tells you *where to look*: the knight that keeps moving and the king still in the middle. But a broken habit is not a refutation. *Rule of thumb:* name the habit, then calculate.

steps.title: Same sacrifice, two positions
steps.prompt: White's knight sacrifice on e5 after two different fourth moves by Black. Predict whether it works in each, then check.

steps.text: A trap works only in the position it was built for. The engine (depth 16) rates the same sacrifice at least four pawns worse after another black move (400 centipawns; 100 centipawns is about one pawn). A remembered pattern is a reason to calculate, never to play. *Rule of thumb:* the move that looks most natural, a capture or a developing move, is the one a trap punishes, so check what it leaves undefended.

steps.prompt: Choose one opening you play. Write the one odd move its opponents sometimes try, name the habit it breaks, and write the reply you would play. Check it in the Openings explorer or with the engine in My games.

title: Moves that help and moves that wait
outcomes: Tells a developing move from a time-wasting move by asking what new work the piece will do

steps.text: A **developing move** brings a piece to a square where it has work to do. A **wasted move** repeats work already done or does none: moving the same piece again, pushing a rook pawn, taking the queen for an early walk. Wasted moves are not banned. They cost time, and time matters when your opponent can use it to attack.

title: Develop, wait or answer: choosing without a label
outcomes: Chooses between a developing move and a non-developing move without being told which kind each is
Names the concrete job that makes a rook-pawn move right: it attacks a pinning piece, takes a square or stops a plan

steps.text: **Moves that help and moves that wait** sorted moves into helping and waiting. Now you choose with no label. A rook-pawn move is rarely best, and it is right when it has a concrete job: it attacks a piece that pins, takes a square the opponent wants, or stops a plan. *Rule of thumb:* ask what the pawn will attack, then compare it with the best developing move.

The job has to be real. A pin does not make every pawn move the best one: compare it with the developing moves. And a plan has to be a plan the opponent can carry out. If you cannot name what the pawn attacks, it is a waiting move, and waiting moves cost time when the opponent can use it.

title: When the position makes a quiet move right
outcomes: Predicts that a pinned knight or a settled centre can make a quiet pawn move the right move
Names the default the move overrides: develop a piece first, or do not waste time on a rook pawn
Sees when the same quiet move costs time because development is unfinished

steps.text: **Develop, wait or answer: choosing without a label** gave rook-pawn moves a concrete job. Here the *character* of the position decides. A pinned knight lets a pawn ask the pinning bishop a question. A settled centre, where neither side has a profitable break, takes the rush out of the game. Each such move overrides a default; name it.

The default to name is the one the move overrides. Against a pin, the default is *develop a piece first*. In a settled centre it is *do not waste time on a rook pawn*. *Rule of thumb:* a pin or a settled centre can make a quiet pawn move right. With no pin and the pieces still at home, the same move costs a tempo.

title: A new move you can explain
outcomes: Explains a novelty as a sound move that leaves known play where it is new to the opponent, and why the engine's first choice need not be one
Finds an improvement on a known move and writes a justification with its engine settings
Says what the app can and cannot verify about a "new" move

steps.text: A **novelty** is a move that leaves known play where it is at least as good as the old move, and is new to the person you play. 'Known' means known to someone: a book, a database, your opponent. Two tests: is it new where it matters, and can you say why it works? The engine's first choice is often already known.

steps.caption: Black to move. A known line: the usual recapture is 5...Nxd5. Model note: reason, Na5 attacks the bishop on c4 (checked); evidence, Stockfish 19 Lite at depth 16 rates Nxd5 at least 80 centipawns worse than the best move (checked); unproven, the lines after 6.Bb5+ c6.

line.say: Na5 attacks the bishop. The knight on f6 stays where it is.
Bb5+ checks and keeps the bishop.
c6 blocks the check and attacks the bishop again.

claims.statement: Na5, Nd4 and b5 are each within 70 centipawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16).
The usual recapture Nxd5 is at least 80 centipawns worse than the best move.
After Na5 the knight attacks the bishop on c4.

steps.text: **What this app can check, and what it cannot.** Its items were checked offline with Stockfish 19 Lite, depth 16, one thread (roughly 16 half-moves). Nothing here can check that a move is new to theory: the Openings page holds online games, not master games. So 'new' here means rare at your opponent's rating. An engine score (100 centipawns is about one pawn) is evidence under those limits, not proof.

A **written justification** has three lines. The concrete reason: a capture, check or threat that the old move allows and yours stops. The evidence with its settings: engine, depth, centipawn gap. What remains unproven: deeper lines, untested replies. **Rule of thumb:** a gap of a few centipawns is not an improvement. If you cannot write the first line, you have an engine move, not a novelty.

steps.prompt: The same known move, 3...Bc5, in two positions that differ in Black's second move. Is there an improvement worth preparing in each? Predict, then check.

It shows no depth and no score for a move you choose, and suggests no novelties. Next: three silent items.

steps.text: The lesson "A new move you can explain" was about one move. This one is about one person. **Preparing for an opponent** asks three questions. Which move will he play? Your best evidence is his own past games; rating-band statistics are the fallback. Does that move cost him something you can name? And what do you play if he does something else? Start with how habits change with rating.

steps.text: **When a prepared reply pays.** Each condition is a rule of thumb. He repeats the move: several of his games, not one. The gap is real: the next-best reply is clearly lower (here, 40 centipawns or more at depth 16). You can reach the position and remember the follow-up. It fails when he plays something else, when your sample is two games, or when many replies score alike. Then rely on understanding; see "Remember the forcing lines, understand the rest".

steps.text: **Ladder of evidence for a prediction.** Best: three or more of his games with the same colour, all with this move. Next: his games in other openings, which show his tastes. Last: rating-band statistics, which describe players like him, not him. Each step down is weaker, so write down which one you used. Then add a plan B: the move you play if he deviates. Predict first, then try one more prepared reply.

title: Remember the forcing lines, understand the rest
outcomes: Tells a forcing line (exact recall) from a flexible position (understanding) by asking whether a natural move loses a lot or many moves work
Finds the different move that each reply to a short forcing line needs

steps.text: Preparation has two jobs. **Exact recall** is for forcing lines, where one slip loses at once: you remember the move. **Understanding** is for flexible positions, where many moves work: you know the plan and the structure. More memorised moves is not better preparation; memory spent on flexible positions is wasted. First, sort two positions.

Real games show which lines are worth the memory. On the Openings page, after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4, Black plays 3...Bc5 in 21% of games at 1100-1300 (869 of 4,100). The engine prefers 4.Nxe5, yet only 29% of White players take it in that band. The line is forcing, and each reply needs its own move. Watch it once.

steps.text: **Exact recall pays** where the line is forcing and you will really meet it. **Understanding pays** where several moves work. **Rule of thumb:** if you forgot the move, could you find it in a minute from principles? If yes, understand it; if no, remember it. Spaced review (the Drill page) fits exact lines best: right answers return after 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 or 32 days; a miss returns tomorrow.
**Two more to sort.** Next: one position where a natural move loses at once, and one where many moves work.

**What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** On the Openings page you can add a line to My repertoire with a one-line note; the Drill page then asks for your move in those positions. title: When the opening habits fail: reasons and conditions
outcomes: States the condition under which each opening habit works: nothing of his own is loose and no threat is pending
Predicts when castling or a developing move is unsound because of the opponent's last move

steps.text: In 'Your first moves' you met three habits: a pawn in the centre, knights toward the centre, castling. Each has a reason, and the reason has conditions. When the reason is missing, the habit fails. In this lesson you test the habits. Predict first, then check.

title: Opening habits: one checked failure each
outcomes: Gives one checked position where taking the centre fails, one where moving a piece again is right, and one where castling is not the move
Says which condition made each habit fail: an attacked square, a loose piece, a pawn that only a trade can leave loose
Recognises a position where none of the three habits fails

steps.text: **When the opening habits fail: reasons and conditions** showed that a habit gives way to a threat. Here each habit gets its own checked failure. Start with the centre. A centre pawn is only as good as the square it lands on, so before you push, count the enemy pieces that attack that square. This is a *rule of thumb*: count first, then push.

Second habit: do not move a piece twice before the others are out. The reason is time, and time is worth little when a piece of yours is loose (attacked and not defended). If the piece that has already moved is the one in danger, moving it again is the development that counts. *Rule of thumb:* a loose piece comes before a new piece.

Third habit: castle early. Castling puts the king away, but it does not defend anything else. Before you castle, ask what a trade could leave loose. A pawn defended only by a piece that can be traded off is the usual case. In the next pair, a position where the d6 pawn defends e5 is set against one where only the c6 knight does.

steps.title: Castle now?
steps.prompt: Black wants to castle in both positions. Predict whether castling is sound in each, then check.

line.say: Black castles.
White trades the bishop for the knight.

The e5 pawn has no defender and White takes it.

steps.text: Conditions, one line each. *Centre:* fails when the square is attacked more often than it is defended. *Moving twice:* right when the piece that moved is the one attacked. *Castling:* fails when it leaves a pawn or piece loose after a trade. All three are *rules of thumb*. The next positions do not say which one applies, and in one of them none fails.

steps.prompt: Pick one of your recent games. Which habit did you follow in the first ten moves, and what did you check about the position before you followed it?

steps.text: Early attacks aim at **f7**: at the start only the king guards that pawn. But an attack with two or three pieces usually fails if the defender develops with tempo, because the attacker has used moves that build nothing. Look at three traps and ask each time: what must the opponent do wrong for this to work?

steps.text: **Bait.** A trap works only if the defender takes it. Before any capture ask: what does my capture open, and what does it take away from my king? In the next position Black can win a queen, and the engine prefers a quiet move.

title: Punishing an opening mistake: find it, or develop calmly
outcomes: Finds the punishment when the opponent's move leaves a concrete target
Develops calmly when no punishment exists
Does not mistake a greedy capture for a punishment
Asks what the last move left undefended or undeveloped before choosing

steps.text: In **Why a quick attack on f7 usually fails** a punishment needed a concrete reason. Now the mistake may be there or not. After the opponent's move ask: what did it leave undeveloped or loose? Do I have a move that uses it now? Does the greedy capture cost me more than it wins? If not, develop. Calm is a good answer. First, an early queen.

**Rule of thumb for the opening:** a punishment needs development on your side and a target on theirs. It fails when the target is defended, when the capture opens your own king, or when the move was simply fine. 'Punish at once' is a misconception: some moves cost the other side nothing you can reach. Next: three positions, one kind of question. Predict first.

title: Punishing an opening mistake: when one change flips the answer
outcomes: Names what a punishment needs (a target with no second guard, a check that works)
Predicts which one-feature change keeps the punishment and which turns it into a blunder

steps.text: In **Punishing an opening mistake: find it, or develop calmly** you decided whether a punishment exists. A punishment rests on conditions: a target guarded only once, a check that works. Change one feature and it can vanish. Your skill now is prediction: say what the plan needs, then look for the one feature that gives it away. First, a position where nothing important changed.

**What each plan needs.** Taking on e5 with the knight is a sacrifice: the f-pawn already guards e5, and after ...fxe5 the queen's check on h5 has to do the work. So the plan needs two things: no *second* guard of e5, and a check on h5 that works. Ask: who else guards e5? Can a pawn block the check? *Rule of thumb:* a defender that adds a second guard of e5 usually ends the punishment; a pawn move on the far wing usually does not. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **Development level.** Two more. In the first, Black has developed one more piece before the same capture. The second is from the Italian opening, where White tries an attack on f7. Look at which black pieces are ready to defend, then predict.

title: A White repertoire: reasons you can say, moves you must know
outcomes: Builds a short White repertoire from the replies his own opponents actually play, with a plan sentence for each
Separates forcing positions, where an exact move is worth remembering, from flexible ones, where the plan is worth understanding
Chooses among several sound moves by the plan he can state

steps.text: A repertoire is a short list of replies to what you actually meet. Start from your own games, not from a book. Write the first three or four moves of your last ten games as White. Count which positions repeat, and build your White replies for the two you meet most.

steps.prompt: From your last ten games as White: which two positions come up most? Write them down. Which one will you prepare first, and why that one?

steps.text: Two kinds of position. In a **forcing** position, one slip loses at once, so an exact move is worth remembering and revisiting. In a **flexible** position many moves work, so learn the plan, not the move order. Spend memory on the first kind and understanding on the second.

steps.title: Memorise or understand?
steps.prompt: In which position would remembering one exact move pay? Predict, then check.

steps.text: **When it holds.** Rule of thumb: if the natural move loses a lot, remember the exact move; if several moves stay close, remember the plan. **When it fails.** You cannot tell from the look of a position which kind it is, and a plan you cannot state is not understanding. Ask: what does this move do?

steps.prompt: Pick one White reply you chose today. Write its plan in one sentence without naming a move. Then write one position where you would need to remember an exact move.

steps.text: A **setup** gives every piece a job: a pawn in the centre, knights and bishops out toward it, the king castled, the rooks joined. It is not a list of moves, because your opponent will not follow your list. The order can change; the reason for each move does not. Here is one White setup with the job of each move. Then you play the next job yourself.

steps.caption: One White setup, move by move. Watch the reason for each move, not the order.

steps.text: A setup is a default, not a law. **Rule of thumb for club play:** when a pawn is offered and a developing move is about as good, develop. Extra pawns cost moves to keep. title: One simple setup with reasons: when the reply surprises you
outcomes: Keeps the reason for each setup move when Black answers differently from the model line

steps.text: You saw one setup move by move in **A setup is a job for every piece**. Now Black stops following the model. The reasons stay: look for the *job* still open (a pawn in the centre, a piece out, the king safe, the rooks joined) and pick the simplest move that does it. A new black move changes the *move*, not the *reasons*. Start with a reply that wastes time.

A pawn on offer is not a job. **Rule of thumb for club players:** when holding a pawn would cost several moves, free your pieces instead. It is only a rule of thumb. It stops applying when taking the pawn wins material at once and the other side gets nothing back. Two positions follow in which Black offers a pawn. Ask what your pieces want, not what the pawn wants.

**When the setup is the right default, and when it is not.** It is the default while nothing is attacked and an equally good simple move exists (a rule of thumb). It gives way to a capture or a threat on the board. And it fits only positions that look like the setups you know. Next: the same kind of question in three positions. Predict first.

steps.text: An opening is a route to a **structure**: the shape of the pawns. Pawns cannot go back, so the shape stays, and it says where pieces belong and which pawn pushes matter. Different move orders can reach the same structure. Learn a few structures and their usual plans, and many openings become one problem.

steps.text: **Carlsbad:** White has no c-pawn, and Black has pawns on c6 and d5. White often pushes the queenside pawns (b4, then b5) to create a target on c6, or trades pieces. Black often repositions a knight toward the kingside or trades pieces. These are usual plans, not laws.

**Isolated d-pawn:** a pawn on d4 with no friendly pawn on the c or e file. Pawns cannot defend it, but it gives space and open lines. The owner usually keeps pieces on and aims them at the king. The other side adds pressure, blockades d5 and trades pieces. Tendencies, not laws.

steps.text: **Open centre:** the central pawns are traded and files and diagonals are open. Speed and king safety count most. Put rooks on open files and develop before you attack. These are tendencies; check what the opponent's last move attacks first.

steps.text: In **Sure material, or a trap?** you were told a position held a trap. Now nobody says. Before a capture, ask two things: *what does it open or take away?* and *what can the other side do next?* If the honest answer is 'nothing', or a reply that you have checked fails, take. title: Blockading a passed pawn: check the square
outcomes: Finds the blockading square and a suitable piece for a passed pawn
Checks that the blockading square is not attacked, above all by a pawn

steps.text:
A **passed pawn** has no enemy pawn in front of it on its file or a neighbouring file. A **blockade** puts a piece on the square directly in front of it, so the pawn cannot advance.
**Rule of thumb:** the default blockader is a **knight**, because it loses no strength standing in front of the pawn. A queen there tends to be driven off; the king belongs in the endgame.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** a blockade works when the blockading square is **safe** and the pawn is dangerous (passed, advanced or central). Check who attacks the square, above all pawns. A piece on a square an enemy pawn attacks will simply be taken.
It is a default, not a duty: if the pawn can be won, win it. A queen can blockade when nothing can hit it.

title: Pawn breaks: ready or premature?

steps.text: A **pawn break** (or lever) pushes a pawn so that it can be exchanged for an enemy pawn. It opens a file or diagonal, or changes the pawn structure. It is also how you attack a chain of pawns: strike at the **base**, the pawn at the back that protects the rest. Judge a break by what it opens and who is ready to use it.

steps.text: A break is ready when pieces stand behind it. Count the defenders of the break square against the attackers, check that no pin punishes the move, and look at what the push uncovers: a pawn that leaves its square can open a diagonal or file for the opponent. In an undeveloped position a break can give the opponent targets. As a *rule of thumb*, finish development first.

title: A free pawn in the centre: break it or restrain it
outcomes: Recognises a free enemy centre pawn: on d4 or e4 (d5 or e5 if the enemy is Black), attacked by none of your pawns and able to advance
Chooses between a prepared break and a quiet set-up of pieces for a given free pawn

steps.text: A **free centre pawn** is an enemy pawn on d4 or e4 (d5 or e5 if the enemy is Black) that none of your pawns attacks and that can advance. You have two answers. **Break** it with a prepared pawn move that attacks it, or **restrain** it: place pieces so that the square in front is covered, and wait. Neither answer always works.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's pawn on d4 is free: no Black pawn attacks it and it can advance.

line.say: The break e5 attacks d4. Two Black men defend e5 and two White men attack it.
White takes.
Black retakes, and White's free pawn is gone. The d-file is open.

claims.statement: No Black pawn attacks d4.
The pawn on d4 can advance.
After e5 the pawn attacks d4.
Two Black men defend e5.
Two White men attack e5.
After the exchange there is no White pawn on d4.
The d-file is open.
e5 is among the engine's top moves.

steps.text: Both answers cost something. A break needs the pieces behind it: count the defenders of the break square against the attackers. Restraint takes several moves and ties pieces to their squares, so it is slow; that is a *rule of thumb*, not a law. Sometimes the break is not ready, and sometimes there is no free pawn at all. title: Connecting the rooks: a step, not a goal
outcomes: Names the pieces that stand between the rooks and the moves that clear them
Connects the rooks when development is otherwise finished
Checks for threats and tempo moves before connecting, and sees when the rooks are already connected

steps.text:
Rooks are **connected** when they stand on one rank or file with no piece of either colour between them. Then each rook defends the other, and they can share a file. At the start the knights, bishops, queen and king are in the way, so connecting is usually the **last step of development**, not the first.
*Which pieces are in the way, and where can they go?*

steps.caption: White to move. Only the queen stands between the rooks on a1 and f1.

line.say: The queen leaves d1. Nothing stands between the rooks on a1 and f1 now: they are connected.
Black strikes in the centre. This changes nothing about the rooks.
One rook goes to the d-file. The rook on f1 still defends it, because nothing stands between them.

claims.statement: At the start the rooks are not connected.
After Qc2 they are connected.
After Rad1 the rook on f1 defends the rook on d1.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** connect the rooks once your other pieces are out and nothing is pending. It is a step, not a goal.
Before you do, ask: *is any piece loose, mine or theirs? Is there a move that makes a threat?* Connecting can also wait on purpose, for instance when castling is delayed. And connected rooks on closed files do little until a file opens.

steps.title: Same position, one rook moved
steps.prompt: In the second position Black's a8 rook stands on d6. Does castling long, which connects White's rooks, still look best? Predict first, then check.
In the last positions, what did you check first: whether the rooks were connected, or whether anything could be attacked? Which should come first?

Connecting the rooks is the answer to none of these; it is what you do when they are all quiet.

steps.text:
Connecting comes last on the checklist. **Skip it** when a piece of yours is attacked and loose, when an enemy piece can simply be taken, or when a developing move also makes a threat. Castling may be delayed on purpose.

**Rule of thumb:** finish development unless something sharper pays.

title: Square control: the whole board at once
outcomes: Reads the n-m counts and the blue or orange tint of the control map on any square
Names what the map leaves out: pins and x-rays
Glances at the map before moving, starting with the landing square

steps.text: Under a lesson board, the **Control map** button paints every square at once. Each square shows two numbers, **White-Black**: how many White pieces and how many Black pieces attack it. **Blue** means White's number is higher, **orange** means Black's. Tap any square to see which pieces they are. Counting attackers is taught in its own lessons; here you learn to read the picture.

steps.caption: White to move. Turn on the map and tap f7.

line.say: The knight joins the bishop. The map on f7 changes from 1-1 to 2-1.

steps.text: The map is a **rule-based count, not a verdict**. A blue square does not mean White wins a fight there; it only says White has more pieces looking at it. Two things it leaves out, on purpose: **pins** (a pinned piece still counts) and **x-rays** (a piece behind another piece does not count). Check both by eye.

steps.title: Same map, different truth
steps.prompt: Both boards show f3 as 0-1 with a black knight on e5. Only one rook has moved. Can the knight capture on f3? Predict first, then check.

steps.text: Make the map a **habit before you move**, in this order. First, the square you want to land on: is Black's number above zero? Second, your own pieces: any whose Black number is higher than yours? Third, a quick look for pins and pieces lined up behind others. It takes seconds and replaces a vague worry with two numbers.

steps.caption: White considers the knight jump to d4. What would the map say there?

line.say: On d4 the map would read 0-2: no White support, two Black attackers.
Black can take with the pawn.

steps.prompt: Which of the three limits of the map (pins, x-rays, 'a number is not a verdict') would you have forgotten? How will you remind yourself to check it?

title: Converting an advantage: take, exchange or stay quiet
outcomes: Lists the kinds of move available when clearly ahead: take material, exchange pieces, make a threat, make a quiet move

steps.text: When you are clearly ahead, the advantage has to be turned into something that cannot slip away. Your kinds of move: **take material**, **exchange pieces**, **make a threat** (a pawn push or piece move that attacks something), or play a truly **quiet move** that keeps his counterplay small. Before you choose, ask: after my move, what is his best reply? The strongest move is not always the one that wins the most.

steps.caption: White to move and clearly ahead. The rook can take the pawn on b7.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn and attacks the queen and the bishop.
The queen steps away.
The rook takes the bishop.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position at least 300 centipawns in White's favour.
After Rxb7 the rook attacks a7 and e7.
Rxb7 is the engine's best move.
Qxb7 is at least 300 centipawns worse than Rxb7.

steps.text: Which kind of move is best depends on the position, so this is a *rule of thumb* and not a recipe. Taking is often best when the capture is also the strongest line. An exchange can be best when it leaves an ending you can judge. A threat can be best when it forces a concession. A quiet move can be best when a capture would give him counterplay. Being clearly ahead still needs moves: check his forcing replies first.

title: Development: a lead you can spend

steps.text:
Development is a lead you can spend. When your pieces are out and the enemy's are still at home, lines open in your favour and his king has few helpers, so a sacrifice that opens them can win.
Before you attack, **count the pieces in play on both sides.** The same sacrifice that wins against an undeveloped army loses against a developed one.

steps.text: The attack is licensed by the lead, not by the sacrifice. Ask: **how many Black pieces are developed, and can his king find a safe square?** If he has a developed defender and a flight square, the sacrifice only loses a piece. A lead also fades: use it before the opponent catches up.

steps.text: Castling early gets the king safe and brings a rook into play. It matters most when the centre can open. When the centre is closed, castling can wait a move or two. Ask: **can the opponent open the centre now?**

steps.text: *Good and bad pieces: now, and later* taught you to find the worst piece. This lesson asks what to do about it. steps.text: An **obstruction** is a pawn or minor piece that blocks the line of a rook, bishop or queen: a file or a diagonal. It can be the enemy's or your own. steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* an enemy obstruction is easier to remove than one of your own, because you can bring many attackers against it. **Count first:** attackers against defenders, including pieces that join after the first capture; the cheapest man should capture first. steps.text:
An open file is a road, not a prize. A rook standing on it does nothing until it can **land** on a square in the enemy camp, best of all on the seventh rank, where pawns and the king are cramped.
Before you double rooks, ask: **which square will my rook land on, and can the enemy cover it?**

steps.text:
The plan works when three things hold.
**Your rook gets to the file first.**
**The entry square is not guarded by a pawn or a minor piece.**
**Something is waiting there:** undefended pawns, or a king with no room.
If the entry square is covered, landing there can cost you the rook.

steps.text:
Sometimes a pawn blocks the file. Count first: if it has fewer defenders than you have attackers, take it with your cheapest piece first.
If another pawn protects it, taking it may only lose material. Players then undermine it with a pawn lever or, rarely, give up material to open the file, but only when the landing square wins at once.

steps.text: **Over-protecting** means giving an important point more defenders than the attack on it needs. The idea comes from a master's writing and is *practical, not proven*. The point should be strong, central and under lasting pressure. The hope is that the defenders stay close to the point and keep their moves. For an ordinary pawn it is simply a lost tempo. In the examples here the extra defender is also a developing move, so the engine's agreement does not show that over-protection itself helps.

steps.text: Ask three questions before adding a defender. Is the point strong and likely to stay under pressure? Does the defending piece keep useful moves where it stands? Is there a developing or active move that does the same job or more? As a *rule of thumb*, if the answer to the first is no, or if a developing or active move does the same job, leave the point alone.

steps.text: This lesson builds on **Passed pawns: blockade early, if you can arrive in time**. A passed pawn gives you three choices: **push** it, **support** it (with the king or a piece), or **hold back** and improve something else. The pawn is an asset, not a duty. title: A pin can last: four ways to meet it
outcomes: Names the four policies against a pinned knight and recognises the question (a flank pawn at the pinning bishop), ignoring and bringing up reserves in play
Checks whether the centre can be opened before asking again
Knows that more than one policy is often sound

steps.text: A pin need not be won at once; it can shape an opening. When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, you have four policies: **put the question** (a flank pawn attacks the bishop), **ignore** the pin and play in the centre, **bring up reserves** so the knight is no longer pinned, or **hold the choice** with a useful move and decide later. (No exercise in this lesson trains 'hold the choice'.)

steps.caption: Black to move. The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen.

line.say: h6 puts the question: the pawn attacks the bishop.
Bh4 keeps the pin. The bishop has answered the question.

claims.statement: h6 is the only pawn move that attacks the bishop.
The engine's first choice is h6.
The queen stands behind the knight.
The bishop on g5 attacks the knight.
e7 is empty, so the knight is pinned to the queen on d8.

steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* the question is good when the bishop's retreat leaves it few squares and the centre cannot be opened with profit, so the bishop cannot come back to life. It is bad when the centre can open, or when the pawn advance leaves your king facing a break. It does not always win a tempo, and it can weaken the side that asks.

title: Ask the bishop only if the centre stays shut
outcomes: Checks whether the centre pawn is already under pressure before asking a pinning bishop a question
Plays or declines the question in an unlabeled opening position, with the centre check as the reason

steps.text: You know the four policies from *A pin can last: four ways to meet it*. Here you decide, from a bare position, whether to ask. Check one thing first: **can the centre open?** As a *rule of thumb*, if your centre pawn (here d5) is already pressed, by a pawn or by a pawn and pieces, it can. Then the bishop may come back to life.

The question is a *rule of thumb*, not a law. It works best when the centre stays shut: the driven bishop finds few squares and cannot return. It fails when the centre can open, or when no pin exists, because then there is nothing to ask. Often several moves are sound, so asking is one option, not a duty.

steps.text: A plan is a **direction**, and it needs a reason: a feature of the position to aim at, such as an exposed king, an open file or a weak pawn. Before you commit, ask two questions. **What is the plan aimed at?** And **can my pieces carry it out** before the opponent can stop it?

steps.text: A plan holds only while its target is there. Move the king and the same attack aims at nothing. As a *rule of thumb*, name the target and the pieces before the first move, and check again after every opponent move. Where a capture or check decides at once, calculate it first; the attack in this lesson was found by calculating, because the target was an exposed king.

steps.text: You already know a plan is a direction supported by a feature of the position (see *A plan the position supports*). Now you choose between plans. title: The difference that decides

steps.text: Before you look for moves, list the **differences between the two sides**: material, king positions, open lines, weak squares. Each difference suggests a possibility. Then ask which one decides the position. A difference does not always favour the side that seems better: here White has the extra pawn, but White also has the exposed king.

The king must take.
Check: the king is hunted and Black mates by force.

steps.text: The method is easiest when the two sides look alike, because then few differences exist to weigh. Counting material is a *rule of thumb*, and an exposed king can outweigh an extra pawn. Change one feature and the verdict can change; change a feature that plays no part and nothing changes. **Ask of each difference: what does it allow?**

title: Better, worse or equal: the valuation sets the mode
outcomes: Labels a position better, worse or equal after listing the differences

Checks a counter-attack before playing it

steps.text: Before you choose a plan, decide **who stands better**. Then match the kind of game to the label (a *rule of thumb*): if you are better, **play actively**, so the advantage is not wasted; if worse, **defend and restore freedom** by bringing pieces into play; if equal, **manoeuvre**: improve your worst piece and do not force matters. The label comes first, and it has to be honest.

steps.text: The label is the hard part. Compare material, then king safety, then piece activity, and say where you are unsure. The mode is a default (a *rule of thumb*), not a law: a worse side may counter-attack, but a counter-attack has to be checked, and an attack from a clearly worse position is the most dangerous choice. An equal position often has several sound moves.

title: Who goes, who stays: allocating pieces to a plan

steps.text: **Allocation** starts with a target: a king, a weak pawn. Decide where the main blow falls, which pieces can go, and which are the minimum to keep at home. *Rule of thumb:* keep the defenders that also do other work (a knight on f3 can guard the king's side and the centre), and do not send everything. With no target yet, there is nothing to allocate.

steps.text: A piece that looks like an attacker may be doing a defensive job (a shield): ask what changes if it leaves. Reserve only the necessary defenders, and recount, because one missed defender turns a winning attack into a losing one. *Rule of thumb:* count the pieces already aimed at the target plus those that can join with a threat next move; attack when that total beats the defenders. If not, improve your pieces first. The counting itself is taught in "Count before you attack: attack now, not yet, or no".

steps.text: *Who goes, who stays: allocating pieces to a plan* taught the shield idea. Now apply it without hints. Before a piece goes forward, ask: **what does it stop the enemy doing from where it stands?** Look along the enemy long diagonals and files. As a *rule of thumb*, send a piece only when nothing is freed behind it. Sending every piece is the mistake.

Here the pawn on e4 blocks the bishop's line, so the bishop does not reach f3 or g2. That is one fact; whether Ng5 works is a separate question. Next, compare boards. steps.text: When both sides have a plan, count the moves each needs and ask who is on move. The side that arrives first usually wins. In a pawn race, count the moves a pawn needs to reach the last rank. A forcing reply can break the count: a king stepping into the pawn's path, or a check when a pawn queens. steps.text: The count is a *rule of thumb*. A king can break it. Draw a square with the pawn and its queening square on one side, as long as the pawn's moves still to go. If the enemy king can step into that square on his turn, he catches the pawn. Blocked pawns have nothing to count, and a queen that arrives with check can win a tempo. title: Prophylaxis: ask what he wants, then decide if it is real
outcomes: Names the opponent's freeing move in a given position by asking what he would play if you passed

steps.text: **Prophylaxis** is a question you ask before you move: what does my opponent want to play next? If the answer is a real freeing move, a quiet move that makes it unattractive can be worth a tempo. It is not passivity. It is also not always needed: when his plan is not real, the question has a quick answer and you carry on.

Imagine you pass and look at his best move. Name what it would do: which pawn it attacks, which line it opens. Then find the quiet move that attacks that square or removes its support. As a *rule of thumb*, stop the break when, if he played it next move, you would lose a pawn or piece or be left cramped. If you would not, carry on with your plan. If he has no break, there is nothing to stop.

title: Restraint: guard the square his pawn wants
outcomes: Names the square an enemy pawn would advance to and says which of your pieces attack it

steps.text: **Restraint** means stopping an enemy pawn break before it happens. Find the pawn and the square it would advance to. If one of your pieces attacks that square, the push is no longer free; whether it costs him material depends on how many defend it. Nimzowitsch's order is a *rule of thumb*: restrain first, blockade next, destroy last. Free centre pawns have their own lesson, "A free pawn in the centre: break it or restrain it".

steps.text: Restraint costs a move, so first check that the break is **real**. Count the attackers of the break square for both sides (a *rule of thumb*, not a law). It fails when his advance is already supported, or when the pawn cannot move at all. Adding an attacker is also not automatically good: the engine's rating of the move still decides. Compare the three positions below.

title: Restraint: is the break real enough to spend a move?
outcomes: Checks whether an enemy pawn break is real (a push backed by a pawn that meets one of your pawns) before spending a move on it

steps.text: In *Restraint: guard the square his pawn wants* you added an attacker to the square an enemy pawn wants. Now ask whether the move is worth a tempo. A break is **real** when an enemy pawn can push to the square with a pawn behind it, and the push would meet one of your pawns. A restraining move, such as a rook behind a closed file, costs a move. Rule of thumb: pay it only for a real break.

steps.text:
A rook on the **seventh rank** (the rank next to the enemy back rank) attacks pawns from behind, since they often stand on their starting squares, and it can keep the enemy king on the back rank.

steps.text: In this app, **space** is counted from pawns only: the squares in the opponent's half of the board that your pawns attack. A white pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6, so enemy pieces cannot use those squares without risk. A square is safe for a piece when no enemy pawn attacks it. More such squares usually leaves the other side's pieces fewer places to go. It is a count, not a judgement: it does not say the space is useful.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A space edge helps most when the other side's pieces really have few safe squares and no pawn can attack your space pawns. If a pawn can, the cramped side may free itself with that lever. Count the squares first, then ask: what can the other side attack with one pawn move? The next three positions differ in one feature.

title: Restrict first, threaten later
outcomes: Prefers a quiet move that denies the freeing break over a showy pawn push when the opponent is cramped
Checks whether a freeing lever exists before relying on a space edge
Recognises positions where pawn space is not a factor

steps.text: In *Space: count the safe squares, then look for the lever* you counted space. Now choose moves. A *rule of thumb*: when the opponent is cramped, first cover the square of his freeing break with pieces, and only then think about threats. A showy pawn push can hand him the freedom you were denying. Restriction is not passivity: it is a plan.

A space edge helps most when the other side's pieces really lack squares and no pawn lever frees them. If a lever exists, the edge does not bind. In an open position with no pawn space at all, space is not the question; piece activity is. Space also does not grow without limit: breaks and exchanges can undo it.

title: Space has a price: the holes and the freeing break

steps.text: In **Space: count the safe squares, then look for the lever** you counted space. Now ask what space costs. Pawns pushed far leave **holes** behind them: squares none of that side's pawns can attack, now or by advancing. The cramped side asks one question: is my freeing lever ready? Rule of thumb: before a lever, check that the pawn it attacks cannot simply punish the push, and that you can recapture on the square it lands on.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A space edge leaves holes, and the cramped side can hit it with a lever. Here White stays better after the lever; it only reduces the edge. A lever is ready when the push runs into no tactic and you can recapture on the lever square (here the queen can, once the e-pawn has left e7). In the second position the e-pawn stands on e7 and ...f6 is rated clearly worse; we know the difference, not the full reason.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The minority attack tends to work when the exchange on c6 leaves a pawn to attack, rooks can use the c-file, the opponent has no quicker threat, and the pawn you push is not simply lost: count its attackers and defenders first. steps.text: A **pawn chain** is a line of pawns that defend each other diagonally. The **base** is the pawn at the back that no pawn defends; the **head** is the pawn at the front. steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Attacking the base works best when the lever is supported and your pieces are ready; attacking the head leaves its defender where it is. steps.text: In this app, **hanging pawns** are two pawns side by side on the 4th or 5th rank, alone on their files and flanks, with no enemy pawn on their files. No pawn can defend them (a static weakness), yet they control squares and can advance (a dynamic strength). Rule of thumb: the plans are to hold them, advance one, or exchange them off.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Advancing tends to work when the advanced pawn gains something concrete, such as attacking a piece, and the pieces that could stop it can be hit. steps.text: An **isolated queen's pawn** (IQP) in this app is a pawn on the d-file with no friendly pawn on the c- or e-file. steps.text:
**Maroczy bind** (app's own definition): White pawns on c4, e4, none on the d-file; Black pawns on d6, g6, none on the c-file (colours may be reversed).

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The bind holds while both breaks stay unready. The cramped side trades pieces and plays ...d5 or ...b5 when the square has enough defenders and a pawn can recapture; counting is the first check, not the whole answer. As pieces come off, it tends to get more room. The owner keeps c4 and e4: pushing either gives up part of the grip on d5.

steps.text: In **The Maroczy bind: what it holds back, and what it costs** you met the bind and its price. title: Switching wings: can the heavy piece cross, and should it?
outcomes: Checks, from the legal moves, whether a rook or queen can change wings in one move
Tells apart three situations: a swing that works, a swing that is possible but bad, and a piece already on the right wing
Does not swing a heavy piece across just because it can

steps.text: A **switch of wing** has three parts. First a demonstration: a pawn advance or threat on one wing. Second, the opponent's pieces move across to meet it. Third, your own rooks or queen swing to the other wing, where fewer defenders now stand. In this lesson the kingside is files e to h. Rule of thumb: it works when your heavy pieces can change wings in a move or two and the opponent is slow to bring defenders back.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black has pushed a pawn to b4 on the queenside, where it attacks a3 and c3: that is the demonstration. White's king is on the kingside. The rook on a8 has not moved yet; the e-file is the first kingside file in this lesson (files e to h).

line.say: Rae8 brings the rook from the queenside to the e-file, one move from the kingside files.

claims.statement: Black has a pawn on b4.
The pawn on b4 attacks a3 and c3.
White's king is on the kingside.
Rae8 is legal: the squares between a8 and e8 are empty.
At depth 16 Rae8 is among the engine's accepted moves (Rae8), all within 0.4 pawns of the best.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A swing needs mobile pieces and an opponent who is slow to answer. It fails if the path is blocked, if a pawn guards the landing square, or if you act on the first threat too early. The app can check legal moves and engine ratings but not the opponent's intentions. The three positions below change one feature at a time.

steps.title: Swing, bad swing, nothing to swing
steps.prompt: Predict which statement fits each position. In the second a Black pawn moved from h6 to h7; in the third White's queen moved from d3 to h3.

Paper exercise (the app does not check it): in one of your own games, find a moment when you had a threat on one wing. Write what a switch to the other wing would have needed, and one reason to wait before cashing in the threat.

title: Switching wings: is the defence really slow?
outcomes: Checks both conditions before swinging a heavy piece: it can reach the wing, and his pieces have not yet come over

steps.text: In *Switching wings: can the heavy piece cross, and should it?* you checked whether a rook could cross. The harder half is the opponent. A switch needs two things at once: **mobile** pieces (the rook or queen reaches the other wing in a move or two) and a **slow defence** (his pieces have not yet come over). If a defender already stands on that wing, the swing usually comes too late. In this lesson the kingside means the e-, f-, g- and h-files. The board shows a swing that works.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's queen and rooks stand on the queenside, and White's rook can reach the f-file in one move.

line.say: Rf1: the rook reaches the f-file, a kingside file, in one move, and at depth 16 the engine ranks it first.

Black's queen is on b6.
A Black rook is on c8.
A Black rook is on d8.
White's rook is on c1.
Rf1 is legal.
At depth 16 the best move is Rf1; Rd1 and Re1 are also within 0.4 pawns of it.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Swing when your piece can reach the wing and his queen and rooks are still elsewhere. It fails when one of them has already arrived, or when you have no demonstration to keep his pieces busy. The app reads piece placement and the engine's ranking, not his plans. Next: the same position three times, with one change each.

title: Aim at what cannot move away
outcomes: Names a target that cannot step aside: a backward pawn whose front square the enemy controls, or a pinned piece

steps.text: Aim at what cannot get away. A **backward pawn** whose front square an enemy pawn controls cannot simply step forward, so you can bring more attackers. A piece **pinned** to its king cannot leave the line of the pin (the pin itself is taught in "Pins: cannot move, or should not move"). A piece that can move away is a poor target for a pawn kick: it moves, and the pawn that kicked it can never go back.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's e6 pawn is behind f5, and the d4 and f4 pawns control e5, the square in front of it. The e-file has no White pawn on it (half-open for White), so a rook or queen can use it.

claims.statement: The pawn on e6 is Black's only backward pawn.
The e-file is half-open for White.
Two White pawns attack e5.
After Qe1 four White men attack e5.
After Qe1 two Black men defend e5.
After Qe1 the queen attacks e6.
Qe1, Re1 and Qe2 are all within a fraction of a pawn of the engine's best move.

steps.text: A target is fixed only if it cannot step aside and the attack can bring more units than the defence. Before you push a pawn at a piece, ask where the piece goes. If it has a good square, you have spent a move and left squares behind. Chasing is not always wrong: it can gain space or send a piece offside. This is a *rule of thumb*.

title: To chase or to fix: choosing the target
outcomes: Counts a piece's escape squares before kicking it with a pawn
Recognises when a pawn kick wins the piece and when it only spends a move
Chooses to fix and attack a target that cannot step aside

steps.text: You can find a target that cannot move (see the lesson *Aim at what cannot move away*). Now compare two ways to use a pawn. You can **chase** a piece, which makes it move, or you can **fix** a target and attack it. As a *rule of thumb*, a chase gains time only if the piece has no good square to go to; otherwise you spend a pawn move and the piece steps aside.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's f7 pawn is backward and cannot move away. Find the way to attack it. The engine rates the position slightly in Black's favour, so this shows how to attack, not that White is winning.

line.say: The queen goes to d7 and attacks the backward pawn on f7. Black's queen can take it.
Black trades queens.
The rook recaptures on d7 and still attacks f7.
Black attacks the rook.
The rook steps to c7 and keeps pressure on f7 and a7.
Black challenges on the c-file.

claims.statement: Qd7 is the engine's best move.
After Qd7 the queen attacks f7.
Black's f7 pawn is backward.

steps.text: Before a pawn kick, count the escape squares. **No safe square:** the chase can win the piece. **A square as good as the old one:** you have used a move and may have weakened your own pawns. A **fixed** target has no escape squares, which is why fixing and then attacking is the safer plan (a *rule of thumb*). Pushing a piece back can still be good play; it has to be checked, not assumed.

title: Transformations: change the structure, check the price
outcomes: Names the exchange that changes the opponent's pawn structure and the pawns that become weak
Names the cost of the exchange (the piece or the bishop pair that goes)
Does not treat damaged pawns as a reason to trade when the engine rates the trade clearly worse
Sees when no capture is available, so no exchange can change the structure

steps.text: A **transformation** changes what the position is made of: an exchange or a break turns one structure, or one kind of advantage, into another. A trade that leaves his pawns doubled or isolated can be worth it, but it has a cost, such as your bishop. Name both before you trade. Which piece to trade is taught in "Trades: which piece goes, which stays"; here the question is what it does to the pawns.

steps.caption: White to move. White can trade the bishop for the knight. Look at what the recapture does to Black's pawns.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight.
If Black recaptures with the b-pawn, Black has doubled pawns on the c-file. The cost to White: the bishop is gone.

claims.statement: A White bishop stands on b5.
A Black knight stands on c6.
Before the exchange Black's doubled pawns are: none.
After Bxc6 bxc6 Black's doubled pawns are: c5, c6.

steps.text: A transformation is only as good as the structure it leaves. The recapture may not be forced, the damaged pawns may be easy to defend, and your own pieces may be the ones that pay. *Rule of thumb:* damaged pawns justify a trade only if you can attack them. Below, the position changes around the same kind of exchange.

steps.title: Worth it, not worth it, not on offer
steps.prompt: Predict which statement fits each position. In the second, a White knight has moved from c3 to g5; the third is a different position. Then name the one change that flipped the verdict between the first two.

title: Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard
outcomes: Marks the holes in one side's camp: squares on its 3rd to 5th rank that none of its pawns can guard by moving forward
Names the enemy piece that could move onto a given hole
Checks that a piece can reach a hole and stay there, not only that the hole exists
Tells a hole from a square a pawn can still guard

steps.text: A **hole** is a square on your 3rd, 4th or 5th rank (counted from your own side) that none of your pawns can guard by moving forward, because pawns never move backward (a pawn changes file only by capturing). A hole is a weakness only if an enemy piece can **reach** it and **stay** there. It is a fact about *your* pawns; your opponent decides whether it matters.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has no e-pawn and his c-pawn stands on c5, so d5 is a hole in his camp.

line.say: The knight settles on d5. No Black pawn can ever attack it, and no Black piece attacks it now.

claims.statement: No Black pawn can ever attack d5.
After Nd5 no Black piece attacks the knight.
Nd5 is among the engine's top two moves.

steps.text:
Before you call a hole a weakness, ask three things.
**Can a piece reach it?** A knight can get there in time; a bishop only squares of its colour.
**Can it stay?** If an enemy knight or bishop attacks it, it can be traded off.
**Is there something to aim at from there?**

title: Holes you can use and holes that only look good
outcomes: Judges whether a hole is usable (reachable and not challenged) or challenged (worth less)
Checks every enemy pawn and piece before relying on a hole

steps.text: A hole is a square your pawns can no longer guard (see the lesson *Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard*). It helps the opponent only if a piece can **reach** it and **stay** there. So a hole gets one of two verdicts: **usable** (reachable and not challenged) or **challenged (worth less)** (a pawn or piece can challenge it, or no piece can get there).

Check three things. **Is it a hole?** None of the pawns on the side that owns the camp can ever guard it. **Can a piece reach it?** **Can an enemy pawn or piece attack that piece on the square?** As a *rule of thumb*, a hole is strong for one side only when its piece can land and stay; the same hole can be worth more in one position than in the next, so check it each time.

title: Holes after a pawn push: who covers them?
outcomes: Predicts the new holes a g-pawn push leaves in front of a castled king
Sees when another pawn still guards a square, so the push creates no hole there
Picks the bishop square that covers the holes a push leaves
Checks whether an enemy knight can land on a hole and stay

steps.text: In **Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard** you found holes already on the board. Now look ahead. A pawn push in front of your castled king makes holes for good, because pawns never move backward. With the e-pawn gone from e7, the push **g6** leaves f6 and h6 unguarded by any pawn. Before you push, list the squares you stop guarding, then ask who could land on them.

steps.caption: Black to move. The g-pawn is still on g7 and the bishop is still on f8.

line.say: The g-pawn passes f6 and h6. No Black pawn can ever guard either square again.
White makes a quiet move. For the moment no Black piece attacks f6.
The bishop arrives on g7 and attacks both holes.

claims.statement: After g6 f6 and h6 are holes in Black's camp.
Right after g6 no Black piece attacks f6.
From g7 the bishop attacks both f6 and h6.

steps.text: A push does not always cost you. If the e-pawn still stands on e7, it guards f6, so g6 leaves only h6. A hole needs a user: it matters when an enemy knight, or a bishop of the right colour, can reach it and stay. *Rule of thumb:* cover the new holes with a bishop or knight before the enemy arrives, or leave the pawn at home.

title: A budget, not an equal share
outcomes: Splits a 15-minute game into an opening share, a middlegame share, an endgame share and a reserve that add up to the whole
Works out how many long thinks a middlegame share allows once routine moves are paid for
Tells a routine, a critical and a forced position apart and says whether a flat share is enough

steps.text: A **time budget** is a plan for where the clock goes: a share for each phase, a reserve for the end, and room to think longer on the few moves that matter. **The same time on every move is not a budget**: it pays as much for a forced reply as for a decision. Every number here is a first guess to test against your own clock.

steps.prompt: A 15+0 game gives each player 15 minutes and adds nothing. Say the reserve is 2 minutes, the opening 3 and the endgame 3. The middlegame is moves 13 to 30, which is 18 moves. Work these out before you read on.

fields.label: Minutes left for the middlegame:
If each middlegame move costs a routine 10 seconds, how many one-minute thinks fit in what is left of the middlegame share?

steps.text: **Pay for routine moves first.** Give routine moves a small price and keep the rest of the phase share for critical moments, such as a tempting capture that may cost material (the pawn grab that loses a queen is an exercise in *How deep? Spend calculation where it pays*; here you only price it). Forced replies cost almost nothing. The prices (10 seconds, one minute) are a rule of thumb to adjust, not a measured optimum.

steps.title: How much of the budget does it deserve?
steps.prompt: Each position comes with the same budget: a routine move gets about 10 seconds. Decide for each: is it critical, so it needs extra from the pool, or routine, so the usual price is enough? A forced move, with one legal move, gets almost nothing; you meet one in the next exercises. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **When a budget works.** It works if you check it: compare your clock at move 12, move 30 and the end with the plan after each game. It fails when rigid: on a critical move, take the minute and pay it back from the share. It barely binds with a big increment (60+30 is about 120 seconds a move over 40 moves). Treat it as a rule of thumb.

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** The app does not time your games, and an imported game is not read for clock times. It keeps no record of time per move. So the budget lives on paper: write your clock at move 12, move 30 and the end. Once you can revise a budget from your notes, you do not need this page.

title: After a loss: judge decisions, set process goals

steps.text:
A result mixes your decisions, your opponent's decisions and luck. After a loss it is easy to blame yourself for everything or for nothing. A habit to try: judge the **decisions** (what you control) separately from the **result**.
This lesson makes no claim about feelings or about what raises ratings.

steps.title: Result and decision are different things
steps.prompt: Judge the decision, not what happened afterwards. Predict, then check.

steps.text: A **process goal** is something you can do whether or not you win: 'run the safety scan on every move', 'write one unsure moment per game'. An **outcome goal** depends on your opponent: 'win', 'reach 1500'. Process goals are specific, in your control and checkable afterwards. They are a habit to try, not a proven method.

steps.prompt: Sort these four goals into process goals and outcome goals.

fields.label: Win my next game

steps.text: **After a loss, a three-step routine to try:** 1. Write one thing you did well. 2. Write one decision you would change and what you could see when you made it. 3. Choose one thing to do differently next session. Do this on paper before you look at an engine or a rating.

**Decide your stopping rule in advance.** For example: stop for the day after two losses in a row. No number is proven; pick one and test it.
The app does not see games you play on other sites, so nothing here runs unless you start it. If a loss leaves you feeling much worse than a game should, talk to someone you trust. That matters more than chess.

title: When you are worse: make it hard, and decide with a reason
outcomes: Lists the resources a worse position can have: a repeated check, a stalemate trick, a fortress, a move that sets a problem
Counts the opponent's winning replies to pick the move that sets the most problems among moves that all lose
Tests a swindle against the opponent's best reply before relying on it
Writes a play-on or resign decision with a reason and knows it is a judgement

steps.text: **Worse is not lost.** When you are behind, aim for the line that is hardest for the opponent, not the slowest loss. Your resources: a repeated check (a perpetual), a stalemate trick, a fortress, a move that sets a problem. Each has exact conditions and each can be tested against the opponent's best reply. Whether to give up the game is a different question: no source gives evidence, so we call it a judgement.

**Exact conditions.** A perpetual needs a safe check at every turn: count the king's squares. A stalemate trick needs two things: the stronger side has no better reply than taking the offered piece, and after that capture the weaker side has no legal move at all. A fortress needs its key squares held. A trap is worth setting only if the right reply costs you nothing (our rule of thumb).

steps.title: A fortress, and one change
steps.prompt: In the first position the defender holds a fortress. In the second, one thing is different. Predict the result each time, then check.

steps.text: No labels now. In each position the side to move is behind in material. Name the drawing resource it offers, or say there is none. Then check it against the opponent's best reply. The perpetual and the stalemate trick are taught in *Perpetual check: the draw you can force* and *Stalemate as a rescue*. The next two exercises are silent.
**Resign or play on?** Our working hypothesis, not a fact: play on while a resource exists and the game still teaches you something; resign when none is left.

steps.text: Players often relax when they are ahead, and a classic slip follows: taking the first gain on offer without asking what the opponent threatens, or whether something stronger exists. **Feeling safe is a risk.** A habit to try: when you are ahead, run the safety scan and look at the opponent's best reply before every move, for ten moves in a row.

steps.text: **When the scan fits.** Use it when you are ahead and tempted to relax or grab. It costs seconds and does not mean refusing every gain: if the scan finds no threat, the capture is cleared, though a simpler way to stay ahead may be better. In a level, tense position the ordinary loop applies. "Ahead" is a rule of thumb: a piece or more, or a clearly better position.

steps.text: **What this lesson claims, and what it does not.** It compares two world champions on a few counted measures, taken from games in our own data: both players rated 2400+, standard games, de-duplicated (The Week in Chess and Lichess broadcasts). It does *not* say who played better, and it gives no verdict on style. A number shows what happened in this sample, nothing more.

**Evidence 1: sample and openings.** Viswanathan Anand: 1,513 games in our data, 1987 to 2026. Vladimir Kramnik: 1,626 games, 2012 to 2025. The windows differ, so the two samples are not the same era. With White, Anand opened 1.e4 in 672 of 762 games (88.2%); Kramnik opened 1.e4 in 277 of 817 (33.9%), 1.Nf3 in 205 (25.1%), 1.d4 in 180 (22.0%) and 1.c4 in 154 (18.8%).
