steps.text: This lesson compares **Magnus Carlsen** and **Hikaru Nakamura** on a few things we can count. It does **not** say who plays better, who is bolder, or what kind of player either one is. Every number comes from our own archive of games where both players were rated 2400 or more, with duplicates removed. Counts and percentages are computed from that file (built 2026-10-29).

steps.prompt: Before the numbers: what is one thing you would want to know about a player's games before saying anything about their style?

steps.text: **Sample.** Carlsen: 5,654 games in our data, 2012 to 2026. Nakamura: 7,612 games in our data, 2012 to 2026. These are the games our archives hold, not everything either player played. Average game length: Carlsen 47.2 moves, Nakamura 48.9 moves. Average opponent rating: Carlsen 2685, Nakamura 2658. Source: docs/player-stats.json.

steps.prompt: Before reading the results, write a guess: which player's draw share in our data is higher, and by how much? Then see whether the next card agrees.

steps.text: **Results.** Draws as a share of all games: Carlsen 1,671 of 5,654 (29.6%), Nakamura 2,226 of 7,612 (29.2%). With White, Carlsen won 1,769 of 2,869 (61.7%); Nakamura won 2,329 of 3,946 (59.0%). With Black, Carlsen won 1,368 of 2,785 (49.1%); Nakamura won 1,806 of 3,666 (49.3%). Both samples are in our data, 2012 to 2026.

steps.prompt: Look at the results card. The draw shares are 29.6% and 29.2%. What does that small gap NOT show? What would you need to check before saying either player draws more?

steps.text: **Queens and openings.** Games that reached move 30 with queens still on: Carlsen 2,716 of 4,948 (54.9%), Nakamura 4,062 of 6,635 (61.2%). First move with White: Carlsen played e4 in 1,234 of 2,869 games (43.0%) and Nakamura in 1,209 of 3,946 (30.6%); Nakamura played Nf3 in 1,234 of 3,946 (31.3%), Carlsen in 277 (9.7%). These are choices in our data, and opponents and preparation shape them.

steps.prompt: Look at the queens-and-openings numbers. Name one reason, other than the player's taste, that could make a game reach move 30 with queens on.

steps.text: **Limits.** We did not count each game's format or opponents; our file only says the games are standard-rate games from two sources (The Week in Chess issues and Lichess broadcasts from 2020). The two players may have faced different opponents and tournaments. Our data holds some of each player's games, so a different archive could give different shares. Queens on at move 30 says nothing about why. Do not turn any number into an adjective.

steps.prompt: Pick one number from the cards, such as the 54.9% against 61.2% of games with queens on at move 30. Write what it does NOT show, and one more thing you would need to check (for example, game format, opponents, or years) before using it to describe how either player plays.

steps.text: **How to read such claims.** Ask four questions. How many games? Which years and which opponents? What exactly was counted? Could the choice have been forced by the situation? steps.text: **What this lesson claims, and what it does not.** It shows a few counts from our own game data for four players: Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, Levon Aronian and Hikaru Nakamura. It does **not** say who plays in which style, and it does not rank anyone. Its aim is the habit of asking, before you believe a number about a player: how many games, from when, against whom?

steps.text: **The sample.** Every number here comes from our data file: games between two players both rated 2400 or more, standard time control, duplicates removed, from The Week in Chess (issues 920 onward) and Lichess broadcasts (2020 onward). It holds *some* of each player's games, not all. For all four players it covers the years 2012 to 2026. Games: Carlsen 5,654; Nakamura 7,612; Caruana 4,963; Aronian 3,796. These counts were produced by our own script from those games; the lesson quotes them exactly and adds no other numbers.

**Evidence 1b: queens at move 30.** Of games that reached move 30, queens were still on the board in: Carlsen 2,716 of 4,948 (54.9%); Caruana 2,924 of 4,516 (64.7%); Aronian 1,761 of 3,307 (53.3%); Nakamura 4,062 of 6,635 (61.2%). steps.text: **A small sample.** Our file also holds Anatoly Karpov, but only 238 games from 2012 to 2022. Queens were still on at move 30 in 108 of 183 games that reached it (59.0%). That is about the same share as Nakamura's 61.2% in 6,635 games, but 183 games could move several points on a few events.

steps.text: The counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 are a **rule of thumb**: a rook for a minor piece costs about two units of material. It is a **sacrifice** only if you can name what you get that lasts: a passed pawn that cannot be stopped, a broken king shelter, a minor piece that dominates, or a blockade. "It looks active" is not a reason. No named gain: keep the rook.

steps.text: In **Giving the exchange: name what you get back** you named the reason for giving a rook for a minor piece. Now decide for yourself whether the sacrifice works. There are three verdicts: **sound** (a check shows it wins), **unsound** (the check shows it fails) and **unnecessary** (a simpler move wins as well). Always test the plain move too.

**What decides it.** The counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 are a rule of thumb: a rook for a bishop costs about two points, so the gain must last. One change can flip the verdict: a defender arrives, or a simpler move does the job. Call a sacrifice *sound* only after a check; otherwise call it *practical* and say you have not checked it.

title: Why give material: the job a sacrifice does
outcomes: Names the job of a sacrifice (decoy, or removing a guard) and states the payoff that pays for it
Counts the king's flight squares and the pieces that can recapture before giving anything up
Tells a sacrifice that fails from one that works after a single change to the position

steps.text:
A **sacrifice** gives up material for something you can name. Two jobs to look for first.
**Decoy:** lure a piece to a square where it hurts its own side.
**Remove a guard:** take or drive off the piece that guards a key square.
Some sacrifices do both jobs at once; say which one you would name first. No named job and payoff means you are guessing. Opening lines against a king: 'The Greek gift: when the bishop sacrifice on h7 works, and when it does not'.

steps.caption: White to move. A decoy: the queen is given up to pull the rook onto g8.

line.say: The queen goes to g8 with check. The knight on h6 guards g8, so the king cannot take it.
The rook takes the queen and now stands next to its own king.
Knight to f7 is checkmate.

claims.statement: Qg8+ Rxg8 Nf7 is a forced mate in two.
After Qg8+ one white piece (the knight) guards g8.

fields.label: The job:
options: Decoy: a piece is lured to a bad square
Remove a guard: a defender is taken or driven off

fields.label: The payoff (mate? material?):

steps.text:
**When a sacrifice holds.** The payoff must survive Black's best reply, including declining. *Rule of thumb:* count the king's flight squares and the pieces that can recapture before you give anything.
**When it fails.** One flight square, or one extra recapturing piece, can turn a mate into a lost queen.
**When it is not needed.** If the material can be won without giving anything up, win it that way.

Two black pieces defend e5.

steps.text:
A count is only as good as its pieces.

steps.text: **When the balance can mislead.** Counting values are a *rule of thumb*. You may stop an exchange early, so read the balance at your best stopping point. The cheapest capturer goes first. title: Counting what can arrive
outcomes: Lists the pieces each side can bring to a pawn's square with one move, and counts again

steps.text:
Counting the attackers and defenders of a square tells you the position **now**. A pawn you push, or one that stays where it is, is also reached by pieces that **arrive**.
So count twice. First count what attacks and defends the square. Then list the pieces of each side that can move to a square from which they attack or defend it, one move each, and count again.

steps.caption: White to move and about to push d4-d5. Watch the count on d5 change as pieces arrive.

line.say: The pawn goes to d5. The knight on e7 attacks it, the rook on d1 defends it: one against one.
Black brings a second attacker: the rook moves to d8.
White brings a second defender: the knight moves to c3. Two against two.
Black takes first with the knight, its cheaper attacker.
The knight takes the knight.
Black could take again with the rook.
The rook takes the rook. Black took a pawn and a knight; White took a knight and a rook.

After the push one white piece, the rook, defends d5.
Black can bring the rook to d8: two attackers.
White can answer with Nc3: two defenders.
Along the engine line White does not lose the pawn.

steps.text:
Three conditions for the second count.
**The target stays.** A piece whose side is to move can step away.
**The arrival is effective.** Not boxed in, and not attacked on its landing square by a piece of lower counting value.
**It arrives in time.** **Rule of thumb:** two-move arrivals usually come too late.
Treat the count as a first estimate: a bigger threat can pull a defender away.

title: Five ways to meet an attack
outcomes: Names the five ways to answer an attack (move, defend, capture, block, counterattack) and uses the first four to save a piece
Saves an attacked piece by a named way, and by any way when none is named
Checks that the chosen way still works against that attacker, and that it leaves nothing else loose

steps.text:
When one of your pieces is attacked and nothing defends it, you have five kinds of answer.
**Move** it. **Defend** it. **Capture** the attacker. **Block** the line (only against a bishop, rook or queen). **Counterattack** with a bigger threat of your own.
List them before you choose. A counterattack works only if your threat is bigger than theirs, so as a rule of thumb look at the first four first.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook attacks the knight on d4 and nothing defends it. Two of the five answers are open here.

line.say: Defend it: the bishop now guards d4.
Black makes a quiet move. Rxd4 Bxd4 would give a rook for a knight.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
After Be3 the engine line does not lose material for White.
The knight could also move to eight squares.

steps.text:
An answer must pass two checks.
**Does it stop the attack?** Defending fails when the attacker has a lower counting value than the attacked piece (a rule of thumb): a pawn takes a defended knight, and you lose a knight for a pawn. A far-away move does nothing unless it threatens more.
**Does it leave something else loose?** A defender that moves can leave the piece it guarded loose.

title: Real threats and fictitious ones
outcomes: Says whether an attack on a piece is a real threat
Names the reason when it is not: a defender, a pinned attacker, or a bigger loss behind the capture
Says that a fictitious threat can become real when the reason goes away
Says 'no threat' when nothing is attacked at all

steps.text:
An attacked piece is not always in danger. A threat is **real** if the capture gains something against best defence. It is **fictitious** if the capture fails. Three common reasons: the piece is defended and the attacker has a higher counting value; the attacker is **pinned to its king** and may not capture; the capture would let you win something bigger.
Ask before you react: **what happens after the capture?**

steps.caption: Black to move. Black's rook attacks the bishop on c4. Is it a threat?

line.say: Suppose Black takes the bishop.
The pawn takes back. Black has given a rook for a bishop (counting values 5 and 3).

claims.statement: One black piece attacks the bishop.
One white piece defends the bishop.
If Black takes, the engine line leaves Black at least 2 behind.

steps.text:
A fictitious threat is fictitious **for a reason**, and the reason can end. A pin lifts when the king steps away. A defender can be driven off or traded. Forget it, and the threat may be real a few moves later.
**Rule of thumb:** check the capture first. If it fails, do not spend a move on it now, but watch for the reason to end.

steps.title: Is the knight really in danger?

title: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?
outcomes: Names the loose pieces of either side
Takes a loose piece, the one with the higher counting value first
Checks for a far-away defender before calling a piece free
Says when there is nothing to take

steps.text:
Remember: a piece is **loose** when an enemy piece attacks it and none of its own side defends it. The enemy can take it for free. Lichess calls such a piece a hanging piece.
Two habits stop most beginner losses. Look at their pieces for loose ones. Then look at your own, after every move your opponent makes.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. No black piece defends d5, so nothing recaptures.
Black has lost a whole knight for nothing.

claims.statement: Only the knight on d5 is loose.
Rxd5 wins the knight.

steps.text:
A loose piece is free only on conditions.
**Count every defender**, including pieces that guard from far away along a file or diagonal.
**Ask what the capture costs.** A piece that has a defender is not free: if the defender can recapture, you may lose more than you win.

Separates a loose piece from one that is undefended but not attacked

steps.text: In "Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?" someone told you to find the loose pieces. Now nobody does. After a move, go through **your own pieces one by one** and end with a number: how many are loose? Zero is a real answer. A piece is loose only when it is attacked **and** no piece of its own side defends it.

steps.text: **Two look-alikes.** A piece that is attacked but defended is *not* loose, although the exchange can still go wrong (see the counting lessons). title: What did their last move threaten?
outcomes: Names what an opponent's last move threatens: a capture, a mate, or a fork
Tells a real threat from an attack that fails after the recapture

steps.text:
After your opponent moves, ask first: **what does that move threaten?** Imagine they get a second move in a row. Could they win a piece, give mate, or fork? Look at what their piece now attacks and what it has just uncovered.
If the answer is 'nothing', you are free to follow your own plan.

steps.caption: Black to move. White has just played ...Re1. What is the threat?

line.say: Black ignores the threat and plays an unrelated move.
...Re8 is checkmate: the pawns shut the king in and nothing covers e8.

claims.statement: White threatens Re8 mate.
No black piece covers e8.

steps.text:
A threat is real only if carrying it out works. Ask:
**What would they take or attack?**
**After my recapture, do they gain?** A rook that takes a pawn-defended bishop loses material.
**Can they really play it?** A covered square or an escape square for my king can cancel it.
Sometimes the honest answer is: no threat.

steps.text: A threat must gain something next move: material or mate. **Rule of thumb** for the list: is a piece of mine attacked and short of defence, can a check lead to mate, can one move attack two things? A covered square stops a fork. An attacked piece that is also defended may still be a threat: a pawn attacking a defended knight is one. Count to be sure.

title: Diagnose: which kind of mistake, and how do you know?
outcomes: Names four kinds of mistake: not seen, seen but miscalculated, misjudged, time pressure
Labels a mistake tentatively from the player's own note
Reads an error log and tests a diagnosis against it

steps.text:
When you lose material, ask which box it belongs in.
**Not seen:** you never looked at the reply.
**Seen but miscalculated:** you looked and the count was wrong.
**Misjudged:** the count was right, your verdict on the position was wrong.
**Time pressure:** the clock decided.
The label is tentative: only the player knows what happened.

Different boxes may need different practice: not seen suggests a scan habit; miscalculated suggests practice with lines and counting; misjudged suggests comparing positions; time pressure suggests a clock plan. This pairing is a hypothesis to test, not a proven rule.

**An error log** lists each mistake with the game, the clock and a box. A diagnosis is a claim the log can test. Fictional log of 8 errors, clock left in brackets: 1 not seen (9:40); 2 miscalculated (7:15); 3 not seen (8:05); 4 time pressure (0:48); 5 not seen (6:30); 6 misjudged (9:10); 7 time pressure (0:35); 8 not seen (7:50).

steps.prompt: Test two diagnoses against this log: 'I lose because I run low on time' and 'most of my mistakes are things I never looked at'.

title: Experiment: change one thing, check fairly, decide by a rule written first
outcomes: Designs a two-way comparison of training methods that changes one thing and keeps the rest fixed

steps.text: An **experiment** changes one thing and keeps the rest the same, so a difference can be blamed on the change. *Example:* practise forks **blocked** (all forks in a row) for two weeks, then forks **interleaved** (mixed with other themes) for two weeks, same minutes, with a check on new mixed positions after each. Two good sessions prove nothing. You need a measure, a check on positions you did not practise, and a decision rule written *before* you look.

In a block of forks you know the idea before you look; a **fair check** does not tell you. Rules of thumb: (1) positions you did not practise, not a mirror of one; (2) no idea named; (3) some positions where the practised idea fails, or 'always fork' scores full marks; (4) the same check for both methods. Compare two methods on one skill, not forks against pins; the order can also fool you (by the second fortnight you know more). Four silent positions follow as a tiny check.

steps.title: The same fork, one change
steps.prompt: A check made only of the first kind of position cannot tell skill from habit. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **How much does a score show?** The My plan page prints a rough range for each score. With 8 items: 2 right is 7%-59%, 4 right 22%-78%, 6 right 41%-93%, 8 right 68%-100%. A start of 3 of 8 and a check of 6 of 8 sounds like a doubling, yet the ranges overlap. 'Cannot tell' means not enough data, not 'no effect'. A plan that shows nothing, or goes down, is still data.

steps.prompt: Press Save note to see the answers. Ranges for 8 items: 1 right 2%-47%, 2 right 7%-59%, 7 right 53%-98%, 8 right 68%-100%. With 4 items, 3 right is 30%-95%. Your four silent answers form a tiny check.

The silent baseline and check use up to 8 positions of that skill (the check from new families), with ranges. For tactics like forks, nearly all are positions where the idea works, so add look-alikes yourself. It cannot compare two methods: keep a paper log. Write your rule in the success box first. Do not delete a failed plan.

title: Lead: your own manual, silent sessions, and handing a skill back by evidence
outcomes: Tells an exercise that shows unprompted skill from one that names the idea
Runs a silent session and records first-try results and which habits he used unprompted
Decides from a small ledger which skill to hand back to coached mode and which has too little data

steps.text: To **lead** is to run the routine yourself while the app only keeps the record. Help should fade on **evidence** that you do something unprompted, session after session. A rating summarises game results; it does not show which habits you use without being asked. A **silent session** turns hints off so that what you do alone shows. Solving an exercise that names the idea shows less than solving one that does not.

steps.title: Same position, the idea named or not
steps.prompt: The board you just saw is the unprompted version of the position you solved, shown with its answer marked. Predict about the named version.

steps.text: **What the record can and cannot see.** The Progress page counts your first attempts at unlabeled exercises (nothing names the idea or the theme): hints used and right without hints, by week, with all skills pooled. Its skill table gives running totals, not weeks. It does not show your habits, your thinking time, or games played elsewhere. So your manual needs a second record, your own: after a silent session, note which habits you used unprompted, and tally results per skill.

steps.prompt: Session note: four silent positions, no hints.

fields.label: How many of the four did you get right on the first try?
Did you run your own routine (for example: list checks, captures and threats) without anything telling you to?
One thing I did that no prompt asked for, or one thing I skipped:

steps.text: **Hand back on evidence.** Handing a skill back to **coached mode** (hints on, lessons and named exercises again) should follow your record, not a mood. The Progress table shows, week by week, how often you used hints and how often you were right without them. **Rule of thumb** (a first guess): judge a skill only after 8 or more hint-free attempts in all, and send it back if accuracy without hints stays under half in both weeks. A small fictional ledger follows.

steps.prompt: Press Save note to see the answers. Fictional ledger, two weeks, first attempts at exercises that do not name the idea. Hints is the share of attempts where you opened a hint; right counts only attempts without a hint. Forks: hints 50% then 10%; right 4 of 6, then 8 of 9. Pins: hints 20% then 20%; right 3 of 8, then 3 of 8. Skewers: right 2 of 2, then 1 of 2. Rule of thumb (a first guess): judge a skill after 8 or more hint-free attempts in all; send it back to coached mode if accuracy without hints stays under half in both weeks.

fields.label: Which skill has too little data to judge?
By the rule, which skill goes back to coached mode?
Forks: hints fell from 50% to 10% while accuracy rose. What does the rule say?
One way this rule could mislead me:

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** Silent practice is a checkbox on the Practice page: hints off, answers shown afterwards. Today lets you set your own aim first, and Progress keeps the weekly record. The thinking prompts for loop levels 1-3 retire after five mixed solves in a row with them closed (five is a first guess). Nothing hands a skill back for you. Saved notes export from Settings, but there is no manual page: keep your manual in your own file.

steps.prompt: Write your manual for one month, with no system prompts: the app only keeps the record. Working alone is not automatically good practice; one study of chess players (reported second-hand, not re-checked here) found practice with others mattered in its sample. So include one thing you do with someone else.

title: Investigate: a claim, a test that could fail, and the limits written down
outcomes: Turns a claim with a source and a year into a question a test could answer, with a result that would show it false
Chooses a tool (engine, tablebase, Openings page, own games) and says what it can and cannot show
Plans the limits and a failing look-alike to write beside a conclusion
Tells a research question from one that a tablebase lookup answers

steps.text: An **investigation** starts with a claim you can name, with its source and year: a book, a video, or a 'rule of thumb' in these lessons. Turn it into a question a test could answer. What would I see if the claim is true, and what would show it false? Pick a tool, write its **limits**, and look for a **failing look-alike**. Checking an old claim counts as research; a novelty is not required.

steps.prompt: Choose a claim to investigate: something you have read, heard or been taught. Write only the claim for now.

fields.label: The claim:
Where it comes from (author or title):
Year:

steps.text: **A worked question.** Claim (made up here, so no source or year): a move that scores well on the Openings page must be sound. If so, moves with equal results should be about equally sound. Data (September 2026 online games, band 1300-1500) after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4: 4.Nxd4 (10,125 games) White won 53%, drew 4%; 4.Ng5 (2,519 games) won 53%, drew 2%. A draw counted as half a win gives 54.7% for both. Now ask the engine.

steps.caption: White to move after 3...exd4. Written beside this result: tool Stockfish, depth 16, one position; data from the Openings page, September 2026 sample, band 1300-1500. At depth 16 the engine ranks 4.Nxd4 first and rates 4.Ng5 at least 1.5 pawns lower. Failing look-alike: 4.Ng5 is a common move (14% of games here) that wins as often as 4.Nxd4 (53% each), yet it is the move the engine rates lower.

claims.statement: Nxd4 is legal.
Nxd4 is the engine's best move.
Ng5 is at least 1.5 pawns lower than the best move.

steps.text: **What each tool can and cannot show.** *Openings page:* what players of a band chose and how those games ended (one month, online); not why, and not strength. *Engine:* a fixed-depth rating of one position; not what people will do. *Your games:* real mistakes, but few. *Tablebase* (seven pieces or fewer; none in this app): exact for each position, so one position is a lookup, not research; a claim about many positions takes many lookups. Write tool, sample, depth and band beside every result.

steps.title: One position, two kinds of question
steps.prompt: The first board has a question the engine can answer. Predict for the second: does a good score on the Openings page answer it?

steps.text: A conclusion is worth keeping when the test could have failed, the result sits beside its tool, sample, depth and band, and one **failing look-alike** is named. It breaks when you keep only the cases that agree, when the sample is tiny (a **rule of thumb**: under about 30 games in a band is noise; the Openings page hides such results), or when a lookup would have answered. A result that contradicts the source is a finding.

steps.prompt: Design the test for your claim. Write what would show it false before you run anything. Notes are saved only on this device and the app sends them nowhere, so show your design to one person and ask them to break it.

title: Back-rank mate, and luft as the cure
outcomes: Finds a back-rank mate
Tells a mate from a check when the king has luft or a guard covers the square
Sees the back-rank threat against his own king
Gives his own king luft with a pawn move

steps.text:
A **back-rank mate** is a check along the first or last rank against a king that is shut in by its own pawns. It works when three things hold: the king has **no escape square**, nothing can **capture** the checking piece, and nothing can **block** the line.
Take one away and it is only a check.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black's rook stands on the open e-file.

line.say: The rook checks along the back rank. The pawns cover the king's escape squares.

claims.statement: ...Re1 is checkmate.
No white piece covers e1.

steps.text:
The cure is **luft** (German for air): an escape square for the king. A pawn move in front of the king, such as h3 or h6, is usually enough. A piece that guards the back rank works too.
Look at your own back rank as well as your opponent's.

steps.title: One pawn move changes everything
steps.prompt: The h-pawn stands on h6 in the second position.
When you check a back rank, which of the three conditions do you check last: escape squares, capture, or block?

title: Back-rank mates for either side

steps.text: You know the pattern from **Back-rank mate, and luft as the cure**. Now it has to work for both sides, with nobody naming it. Before each move ask two questions. Can I check on the enemy first rank, and is that mate? Could the opponent do it to me: does my king have a free square, and does a piece of mine guard my first rank? Look at both kings, every time.

steps.caption: White to move. What does Black threaten, and how can White answer?

line.say: White makes a luft with the h-pawn, so the king gets the square h2.
Black checks on the first rank.
The king steps out. It was only a check.

claims.statement: If White passed, ...Re1 would be checkmate.

steps.text: A back-rank mate needs three things together: **no flight square**, **nothing that can capture the checking piece**, and **nothing that can block**. For your own king the same list is a checklist: one guard on the first rank, or one free square, removes the threat. As a **rule of thumb**, make air once a threat appears rather than on every move, because it costs a move and loosens the pawns. Predict before you look.

steps.prompt: Only one feature changes each time. Predict whether White threatens mate.

title: Clearance: step aside with a threat
outcomes: Finds the vacating move that carries a threat when told to clear a line
Checks what the cleared piece attacks once the line is open
Rejects a vacating move that has no threat, or that opens a line leading nowhere

steps.text:
A **clearance** is a move that takes a piece off a square or a line so that another piece can use it. It usually works only when the vacating move **carries a threat of its own**, such as a check or a capture: the opponent must answer it and has no time to cover what you opened.
Opening a line is not enough by itself.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight on f2 stands on the f-file between the rook on f8 and the first rank. The knight on e3 covers f1 and g2.

line.say: The knight moves with check and leaves f2 at the same moment. The f-file opens for the rook.
White takes the knight. (If the king steps to h1 instead, Rf1 is mate as well.)
The rook goes down the open file. Rf1 is checkmate.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Nh3+ (depth 16).
Nh3+ forces checkmate in 2 or fewer against the engine's best defence.
While the knight stands on f2, the rook on f8 does not reach f1.
After the knight has left f2, the rook on f8 attacks f1.
The knight on e3 covers f1 and g2.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the vacating move makes a threat, and the cleared line leads somewhere that matters, such as a square the queen can use.
**When it fails:** the target square is defended, or the line is blocked further on, or the piece behind is not on the line at all. **Rule of thumb:** a vacating move with no threat gives the opponent time to close the line again.

title: Clearance: win, mate, or only retreat?
outcomes: Finds the vacating move that opens a line and wins material or mates, in a mixed set
Tells a forcing vacating move from one that only retreats

steps.text:
This lesson follows **Clearance: step aside with a threat**. Many moves open a line; few are worth playing. Ask three things.
**1. Is the vacating move forcing?** A check, or a capture with check, leaves the opponent no time.
**2. What does the opened line reach?** It should lead to mate or to material.
**3. Is the king's flight covered?** A free square can make the attack fizzle.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook on f8 stands on the square the queen wants.

line.say: Rh8+ is check, and the rook leaves f8 with tempo.
Black must answer the check; here the rook interposes on h7.

The king steps to g6.
Rg8+ is check on the g-file. Black can take it with the queen, and that loses the queen.
The queen takes the rook.
Qxg8+ wins the queen for a rook, with check again.

After Rh8 the rook gives check to the king on h6.
Along the engine line White ends material ahead.

steps.text:
**It works when** the vacating move is forcing and the opened line reaches a king with no flight square, or a piece that cannot be defended. **Rule of thumb:** list the moving piece's checks and captures first.
**It fails when** no piece stands on the opened line, or the king gets a free square once the exchanges end.

steps.text: This lesson builds on **Clearance: step aside with a threat** and **Clearance: win, mate, or only retreat?**. A clearance needs a vacating move the opponent must answer, and a line that leads somewhere. Test it by *removal*: take the threat away in your head, or the piece that would use the line. If the opponent gets a free move, or the line leads nowhere, the idea fails.

steps.caption: Black to move. The rook on f5 stands in front of its own queen.

line.say: Rf1+ is check, so White has no time to cover f3.

steps.text:
**The removal test.**
**1.** Name the threat of the vacating move: a check, a capture, or an attack on something bigger.
**2.** Name what the opened line reaches.
**3.** Remove one of them and ask: does the opponent now have a free move to cover?
**Rule of thumb:** a vacating move with no forcing threat usually hands the opponent a free move, and the clearance fails.

title: Combinations: a chain of forcing moves, checked to the end
outcomes: Names the links of a short combination (for example removing a defender, then a mating pattern)
Finds a two-motif sequence when told a combination exists
Plays the sequence to the last position and checks the opponent's replies

steps.text: A **combination** is a chain of forcing moves in which each move is justified by the next. It usually joins ideas you already know: a fork (*L-TAC-FORK-1*), a pin (*L-TAC-PIN-1*) or removing a defender (*L-TAC-REMOVE-DEFENDER-1*), ending in a mating pattern or a won piece. The first move may look bad. The last move pays for it.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook on c8 guards the back rank.

line.say: Qxc8+: the queen takes the rook that guards f8. This removes a defender.
Black takes the queen. Any other reply also loses to mate in two (engine).
Rf8#: nothing guards f8 now. A back-rank mate ends the chain.

claims.statement: A black piece (the rook on c8) attacks f8 at the start.
After Qxc8+ Bxc8 nothing black attacks f8.
Qxc8+ forces checkmate in two.
Qxc8+ is the engine's first choice.

steps.text:
Check the whole chain, not only the first move. Play it to the last position. At every step ask what else the opponent can do: a quiet reply, a check, or declining the capture.
A combination that beats weak defence can fail against the best defence. *Rule of thumb:* if a simple move wins, play it; a complicated course adds risk.

title: Decoy: luring a piece to a bad square

steps.text: A **decoy** is a sacrifice that lures a piece, often the king, to a square where it can be hit. The opponent is better off taking, and the capture puts the piece where you want it. Ask: which piece do I want on which square, and what makes it go there?

steps.caption: Black to move. The white queen on e4 is defended by the king on e3. Other king moves lose to mate, so taking is White's best try.

line.say: The rook offers itself with check.
The king takes the rook and leaves e3.
The queen takes the queen with check.

claims.statement: ...Re2+ followed by ...Qxe4+ wins material along the engine line.
Only the king on e3 defends the queen on e4.

steps.text: A lure needs two things. **The capture must be forced**, or at least better than every other reply. **The follow-up must win at once** on the new square. If the opponent can decline, or another piece can take the offer, the sacrifice is just a lost piece.

steps.title: Another piece can take
steps.prompt: The white rook stands on d2 instead of d3, so it can take on e2 as well.

steps.text: **When it holds:** the offered piece must be taken and the lured piece lands where the follow-up wins. **When it fails:** the offer can be refused, the follow-up line is blocked, or the lured piece has a flight square. As a rule of thumb, check every reply that does not capture.

steps.text: A defender can be **forced away** rather than captured. A check, a capture or a threat that it must answer pulls it off its key square, and what it was guarding falls. This is *deflection*. Ask: what is the piece guarding, and what forces it to leave?

Deflection works when the defender has no good alternative. Before you play it, ask two questions. **What if the defender refuses?** A check cannot be refused, but a capture or threat can be, so see what you win then. **Does another piece take over the duty once the first has gone?** If yes, the idea fails.

steps.prompt: A white bishop stands on d3, where it also covers f1.

steps.text: **When it holds:** the move forces the defender, and the square or duty it leaves is unguarded the moment it goes. **When it fails:** the defender can decline without losing anything, or a second piece covers the same square. As a rule of thumb, list every guard of the target before you start.

steps.text: In **Deflection: forcing a defender away** you were told to pull a defender away. Now the position is unlabeled. A deflection needs a defender that *must* move, and a duty that nobody else can take. A check must be answered, so a check can force a piece. A mere offer can be refused. Solve this position, then follow the line.

line.say: The rook checks along the first rank.

steps.text: A **desperado** is a piece that will be lost whatever you do. Before it goes, let it capture as much as it can. When one of your pieces is attacked and every square it can reach is attacked too, ask what it can take on the way out. It cannot be saved, so each capture cuts the loss.

After Nc5 the knight on c5 is attacked (by the pawn on d6) and no white piece defends it.

steps.text:

**Is it really lost?** If it has a safe square, saving it may be better. A defender does not help against a pawn.
**What does each capture allow?** Count the recaptures, and compare with losing the piece for nothing.

steps.text: A forced mate is found by **listing**, not by hoping. List every check. For one check, list every reply: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king. The check starts a **mate in two** only if you have a mating move against *every* reply. Here we test checks only: if every check fails, a quiet first move may still mate (next lesson).

steps.text: **Why the list matters.** A check can fail in three ways: the defender takes the checking piece, a block spoils your next move, or the king has a step you did not count. *Rule of thumb:* before you call a check a mate in two, try to take the checking piece with each enemy piece, king included. A capture is fine only if you still have a mating move after it.

title: Mate in three: the same list, one round deeper
outcomes: Follows a first move through each reply to the mate in three
Counts the king's legal moves after the first move before following a line
Rejects a mate in three that one extra king square breaks
Says "no forced mate in three" when a promising check fails

steps.text: A **mate in three** adds one more round: your move, their reply, your move, their reply, mate. Use the same list at each of your turns. After your first move, test the defender's forcing replies first: a check, the capture of your attacking piece, a move that gives the king a square. *Rule of thumb:* count the replies after the first move. If there are only one or two, follow each to the end.

steps.caption: White to move. Bxc5+ starts a mate in three. Count the king's moves after each check.

line.say: Check. The black king has one legal move.
Ka8 is forced.
Check again, along the long diagonal.
Black blocks with the bishop.
The bishop takes the blocker. Checkmate.

claims.statement: Bxc5+ forces checkmate in three.
After Bxc5+ the black king has one legal move.

steps.text: **Where the search breaks.** The defender has more chances: a check, the capture of your attacking piece, or a king square you did not count. One extra square can end the line. *Rule of thumb:* after the first move, count the king's squares and the defender's checks before following any line. A strong attack is not a mate: if the list runs out, say "no forced mate" and look for another plan.

title: Named mates and the conditions behind them
outcomes: Finds smothered mate, Arabian mate and the queen-and-bishop mate on h7
States the conditions each mate needs
Tells a mate from a check when one condition is missing

steps.text:
Some mates have names because they recur. Each name is a short list of conditions: where the king stands, what blocks its squares, and which piece protects the checker.
Learn the conditions, not only the picture. If one condition is missing, it is just a check.

steps.caption: White to move. The black king is shut in by its own rook and pawns.

line.say: The knight gives check and nothing can capture it. This is smothered mate.

claims.statement: Nf7 is checkmate.
It is White's move and the game is going on.

steps.text:
Every named mate answers the same questions about the checking move.
**Can the king move?** Count its free neighbours.
**Can the checker be captured?** By which piece?
**Can the check be blocked?** (A knight check cannot.)
A missing condition turns the mate into a check.

title: Is there a tactic at all?
outcomes: Checks that the piece making a tactic can survive before playing it
Tells a real tactic from a pattern whose key square is covered or undefended
Says when a position is quiet and no tactic exists

steps.text:
Before you play a clever-looking move, check that a tactic exists at all. Many positions have none.
List your **checks, captures and threats**. For each, ask what your opponent's best reply is, above all whether the piece you moved can simply be taken.

steps.caption: White to move. A pawn can fork the king and the rook, but look at the square.

line.say: The pawn gives check and attacks the rook.
The king takes the pawn. Nothing defended f4.

claims.statement: f4+ gains nothing along the engine line: the king takes the pawn.
No white piece defends f4.

steps.text:
A pattern on the board is not a tactic until it passes three checks.
**Can the piece I move be taken?** A covered square ruins a fork.
**Does the target really fall** after the best reply?
**Is a quiet move better?** If no forcing move works, improve your worst piece.

title: A familiar pattern is a suspect, not an answer
outcomes: Answers 'none' correctly in mixed sets with no named tactic
Spots when a familiar pattern fails because its key square is covered or its target has moved
Finds the better move when the familiar pattern fails and a different tactic exists
Falls back to a safe move or a plan when nothing forcing exists

steps.text: In **Is there a tactic at all?** you answered yes or no for a named tactic. Now the sets are mixed. Many positions have no tactic, some show a pattern you know that fails, and some hide a different tactic. A familiar pattern is a cue to check, not an answer. See a pattern work, then judge a position.

steps.caption: White to move. A knight fork is available.

line.say: The knight checks the king and attacks the queen on c8.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the queen.

claims.statement: Ne7+ is the engine's first choice.
Ne7+ followed by Nxc8 wins the queen.
Nothing black covers e7.

steps.text: **Treat a familiar pattern as a suspect.** Check the square it needs: is it covered? Check the piece it targets: is it where you think? If the pattern fails, ask once more whether a different forcing move exists (checks, captures, threats). If not, a safe developing move or a plan is the right answer. Many positions in real games have no tactic.

title: Overloaded defenders
outcomes: Finds a piece that defends two things and the move that exploits it
Lists every job of a defender before attacking it
Says why a second defender or a shared line cancels the idea

steps.text: A piece with **two jobs** can be beaten. If one defender guards two targets, attack one: when it answers there, the other is left alone. This is an *overloaded defender*. Ask: which piece guards two things, and can it keep both?

Not every piece with two jobs is overloaded. **List all its jobs.** Then ask whether they are both needed at once, and whether one move of the defender or a block can serve both. Only a defender forced to choose is overloaded.

steps.title: A second defender of the rook
steps.prompt: The white king stands on b1 and also defends a2.

steps.text: **When it holds:** both jobs are needed now and one move cannot do both; your move forces a capture or check. **When it fails:** another piece shares a job, or the jobs lie on one line. As a rule of thumb, count the defenders of each target, not just the one you attack.

steps.prompt: When you thought a piece was overloaded, did you list every job it had and every other defender?

title: Perpetual check: the draw you can force
outcomes: Finds the check that starts a perpetual when the side to move is behind
Plays the checking line until the position repeats
Counts the king's flight squares and checks that the queen cannot be captured
Does not take a perpetual when a better move exists

steps.text: A **perpetual check** is a series of checks that the king cannot escape, so the same position keeps returning. When a position occurs three times, a player can claim a draw. When you are worse, a perpetual can save half a point. It needs every reply to lead back into more checks, so **test the king's squares** first.

steps.caption: White to move. Black is ahead (a queen and three pawns against a queen), so White looks for checks.

line.say: The queen takes a pawn with check. The king has only one legal move.
Forced: g8 and g7 are covered by the queen.
Check again. The king has one square again.
Forced. The queen can go back to f7.
The position after the first check is back, for the second time. A third time allows a draw claim.

claims.statement: Qxf7+ is the engine's first choice.
The engine rates the position as equal (depth 16).
After Qxf7+ the king on h7 has exactly one legal move.
No black piece attacks the queen on f7.
After Qxf7+ Kh8 Qf8+ the king on h8 again has exactly one legal move (h7).
After five moves the queen is on f7 again.
And the black king is on h7 again.

steps.text:
Three tests before you rely on a perpetual.
**Where can the king go?** Count its flight squares after each check.
**Can the checker be captured, or the check blocked?**
**Is the draw really your best result?** If another move wins, or the perpetual is not there, a draw may be a mistake. *Rule of thumb:* take the perpetual only when the alternatives are worse.

steps.title: Does the perpetual still hold?
steps.prompt: First position: the perpetual works. Second: a black rook now guards f8. Third: White has an extra knight. Predict, then check.
Before you played a check in the silent items, did you count the king's squares, or did the checks just look promising? Write what you did.

fields.label: Did you count the king's legal moves after the check?
What surprised you, if anything? (one line)

title: Perpetual check: test the king's squares first
outcomes: Finds the perpetual check for the side that is worse in a mixed set of positions
Lists the king's escape squares and the blocks and captures before relying on the checks
Says which feature of a position stops a series of checks from repeating

steps.text:
This lesson follows **Perpetual check: the draw you can force**, where you were told to find the perpetual. Now nobody tells you. You are the side that is behind, and you must look for the checks yourself.
A row of checks is not yet a perpetual. It becomes one only if the king cannot leave the checks, nothing can block or capture the checking piece, and the position repeats.

**Test before you rely on it.** (1) List your checking moves. (2) For each one, count the king's squares and ask whether anything can block or capture the checker. (3) Find your next check: is its square guarded? Only if every answer leaves you another check do the checks repeat.
**Rule of thumb:** a king boxed in by its own pawns is the usual sign; a guard of the checking square breaks it.

steps.title: Same checks, one change
steps.prompt: White is behind in material in all three. Same first check, one change each time. Predict, then check.

title: Pins: cannot move, or should not move
outcomes: Tells an absolute pin (no legal move) from a relative pin (legal but costly)
Wins a pinned piece by attacking it again
Checks that something valuable really stands behind the pinned piece
Tells a pin from a fork

steps.text:
A **pin** attacks a piece that cannot, or should not, move, because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line.
In an **absolute** pin the piece behind is the king, so moving the pinned piece is illegal. A pinned piece is easy prey: it cannot run away from a second attacker.

steps.caption: White to move. The black bishop on e6 stands between the rook and the king.

line.say: The pawn attacks the bishop. It is pinned and cannot leave the e-file.
Black moves the king, but the bishop is still attacked.
The pawn takes the bishop. White has won a bishop for a pawn at least.

claims.statement: f5 wins the bishop along the engine line.
The rook on e1 attacks the bishop.

steps.text:
Two kinds of pin.
**Absolute:** the king is behind. The pinned piece has no legal move.
**Relative:** something valuable, but not the king, is behind. The piece may legally move, but then it loses what stood behind it.
'Cannot move' and 'should not move' differ. A **fork** is one piece attacking two targets; a pin needs a line with something behind.

steps.title: Is the piece really pinned?
steps.prompt: In the second position the king stands on d8.

steps.text: Some pins win nothing at once. A pinned piece stays tied to its square and is a poor defender, which can shape play for many moves. Whether that matters is judged case by case, and later strategy lessons return to it.

steps.prompt: Which part is least clear: telling an absolute pin from a relative one, or checking that something valuable really stands behind the pinned piece?

title: Is the pin real, and can you win the piece?
outcomes: Judges whether a pin is real by asking whether the pinned piece may still move on the line
Wins a pinned piece by adding attackers, using the cheapest attacker first
Predicts how one extra defender changes the count

steps.text: From **Pins: cannot move, or should not move** you know what a pin is. Now judge whether it is real and how to win the piece. A knight pinned to the king cannot move at all. A pinned rook or bishop may still slide along the pin line, even capture the pinner. The best attacker of a pinned piece is a **pawn**, because the piece cannot run.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on d5 is pinned to the king by the rook on d1.

line.say: The pawn attacks the pinned knight. The knight cannot move away.
The king steps off the file, ending the pin, but it is White's move.
The pawn takes the knight.

claims.statement: The knight has no legal move: it is pinned.
e4 wins the knight along the engine line.

steps.text: To win a pinned piece, multiply attackers and count: attackers against defenders, cheapest capture first. **Rule of thumb:** one extra defender can turn a win into an even trade, so recount whenever the position changes. Also check whether the pinned piece can slide along the line: if it can, it is only half pinned and an attack does not trap it.

steps.title: One more defender
steps.prompt: Only a black pawn has been added. Predict whether Nxd5 still wins material.
Before you attacked the pinned piece, did you check whether it could move along the line, and did you recount the defenders? (low / medium / high confidence)

title: The quiet move: no check, no capture, still decisive
outcomes: Recognises a quiet move: no check, no capture, yet decisive
Finds the quiet move when told there is one
Checks the opponent's free replies (checks and captures) before trusting a quiet move
Prefers a forcing win when one exists

steps.text: Not every winning move is a check or a capture. A **quiet move** gives no check and takes nothing, yet it prepares a threat the opponent cannot meet, or it removes their last defence. Look for one when the forcing moves have run out. It is a move to find, not one to play by habit.

steps.caption: White to move. Look for a move that is neither a check nor a capture.

line.say: Rh1: no check, no capture. The rook lines up behind the queen, so Qxh7 would be mate.
Black has no defence that works; the engine finds this best.
The queen takes on h7 with checkmate.

claims.statement: Rh1 is legal.
The rook goes to an empty square: no capture.
No white piece attacks the king on h8 after Rh1: no check.
Rh1 forces checkmate in two.
Rh1 is the engine's first choice.

steps.text:
A quiet move gives the opponent a free move. Before you play one, ask:
**Does the opponent have a check or a capture that wrecks it?**
**Does a forcing line already win?** If so, play that; a showpiece is not a better move.
*Rule of thumb:* look at checks, captures and threats first, then at quiet moves.

steps.title: Does the quiet move still work?
steps.prompt: The first position is a quiet move that wins. In the second, a pawn has moved so that Black gets a strong reply. In the third, a pawn gives White a forced mate. Predict, then check.
When you looked for the quiet move, did you first check what the opponent could do with a free move (a check or a capture)? Which of the two was easier to forget?

title: The quiet move in a combination
outcomes: Searches an unlabeled position in a fixed order: checks, captures, threats, then a quiet move
Finds the quiet move when the forcing moves do not win
Does not play a quiet move when a forcing line already wins
Checks the opponent's free reply before trusting a quiet move

steps.text:
This lesson builds on **The quiet move: no check, no capture, still decisive**. There you were told a quiet move existed. Now nobody tells you. Use a fixed order:
1. List your checks.
2. List your captures.
3. List your direct threats.
4. Only if none of these wins, look for a quiet move.
5. Then give the opponent a free move and find their best check and capture.

steps.caption: White to move. Run the order: is there a check or a capture that wins? If not, which calm move?

line.say: Qh5: no check, no capture. It threatens Qh7+ with the knight on g5 behind it.
Black attacks the knight on g5, but the queen is not attacked.
Qh7+ is check, and the queen is protected by the knight. Against this defence White nets at least eight points.

claims.statement: Qh5 is legal.
The queen goes to an empty square: no capture.
No white piece attacks the king on g8 after Qh5: no check.
Qh5 is the engine's first choice and the next move is far worse (depth 16).
Along the engine's best line Qh5 nets White at least eight points of material.
After Qh5 Rf5 Qh7 the queen gives check to the king on g8.

steps.text: A quiet move earns its place only when two things are true. **First**, the forcing moves do not win. **Second**, the opponent's free move (best check, best capture) does not hurt. *Rule of thumb:* when a forcing line wins by force, it is usually the safer choice; the quiet move then adds nothing. A quiet move that leaves a piece attacked can lose on the spot.

title: Removing the defender
outcomes: Finds the capture that takes away the only defender of a piece
Counts the defenders of the target before capturing one
Says why a second defender or a cheaper recapture defeats the idea

steps.text: A defended piece is only safe while its defender stays. If one piece does all the defending, **capture that defender** and the target is left without protection. This is *removing the defender*. It is a capture, so it is the plainest of the ways to attack a defence. Look for the defender first, then ask what captures it.

Taking the defender is a trade, and a trade can go wrong. Before you capture, count: **who else defends the target?** And **what can recapture on the square you capture on?** The idea works only if the target ends up with no defender after the exchange.

steps.title: A second defender
steps.prompt: A white pawn on f2 now guards g3 as well.

steps.text: **When it holds:** the target has one defender and you can capture it; after the trades the target is still unprotected. **When it fails:** a second piece defends the target, or the defender is guarded so that your capture loses more than it wins. As a rule of thumb, count both before you take.

steps.prompt: When a piece looked defended, did you count every defender before you captured one?

title: Removing the defender: does it really win?
outcomes: Finds the capture of a defender that wins material when the theme is not named
Recounts the target square after the removal before playing it

steps.text:
In *Removing the defender* you found the capture that takes a sole defender. This lesson is about deciding whether to play it. Two questions before you capture the defender:
**Does another piece take over its job?**
**After the whole exchange, am I ahead?**
A capture that only trades pieces wins nothing.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on e7 is guarded by the queen on d8.

line.say: The queen takes the guard of the knight on e7.

The knight lost its guard, so the rook takes it.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Qxd8 (depth 16).

steps.text:
**When it works:** the defender is the only guard of the target, and after every recapture you have won more than you gave up. Use the counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 (a rule of thumb, not true worth) to add it up.
**When it fails:** another piece guards the target after the removal, or the exchange is an even trade. Recount the square, including every recapture.

title: Skewers: the king moves, the piece behind falls
outcomes: Finds a skewer when told to look for one
Checks that the front piece cannot capture the attacker
Checks that taking the piece behind gains material
Says when a check lines up nothing

steps.text:
A **skewer** is a pin in reverse. You attack a valuable piece that has to move, and the piece behind it on the same line is left to be captured.
The commonest form is a check: the king must step aside, and what stood behind it falls.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white king stands in front of the knight on a2.

line.say: The bishop checks the king along the diagonal. The knight stands behind it.
The king must move out of check.
The bishop takes the knight.

claims.statement: ...Bd5+ followed by ...Bxa2 wins the knight.

steps.text:
Before you skewer, ask:
**Can the front piece capture my piece?** A king next to your bishop takes it unless it is defended.
**Does taking the piece behind gain material?** If it is defended and its counting value is no higher than your attacker's, you only trade.
Then check that nothing can step in between.

steps.prompt: Only the white rook has moved: from d1 to g1.

title: Skewers when nobody says skewer
outcomes: Finds a skewer in a mixed set when no theme is named
Rejects the skewer when the piece behind the king is defended
Rejects it when the piece behind is not on the line
Answers 'no tactic' when a check lines nothing up

steps.text: In **Skewers: the king moves, the piece behind falls** you were told to look for a skewer. Now nobody says so. A check that lines up a piece behind the king is a *candidate*. It wins only if the piece behind is undefended or has a higher counting value than your attacker, and nothing stands in the line. Count before you play it. Try this position, then see the line.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white king on f3 has a rook on f8 behind it.

line.say: The rook checks along the f-file. The white rook on f8 stands behind the king.
The king must leave the file.
Black takes the rook on f8.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is among the accepted moves, and every accepted move is within 40 centipawns of it (depth 16).
Along the engine's best-defence line, Rf1+ nets Black at least 5 points of material (pawn 1, minor piece 3, rook 5, queen 9).
The Lichess tablebase (exact for 7 pieces or fewer) confirms that Rf1+ wins for Black.

steps.text:
**Before a skewer, three questions.**
1. Is the piece behind on the line, with nothing between?
2. Is it defended? If so, compare what you take with what you lose, using the counting values (1, 3, 3, 5, 9) as a rule of thumb.
3. Can the front piece capture your attacker, or step aside with a check?
If an answer is bad, look elsewhere.

title: Stalemate as a rescue
outcomes: Finds the sacrifice that forces a stalemate when told to look for one
Counts the legal moves left to the side that would be stalemated
Sees that a spare pawn move, or a king with room to move, ends the trick
As the stronger side, avoids the move that stalemates

steps.text:
In **stalemate** the side to move has no legal move and is not in check. The game is a **draw**: neither side wins.
So a side that is clearly losing can sometimes save the game by giving up a piece, usually with check, so that the capture leaves it with no legal move. The stronger side must check, before each quiet move, that the opponent still has a legal move.

steps.caption: Black to move. White has a queen, Black only a rook, and Black's king on c8 has no free square.

line.say: The rook goes to a7 with check, next to the white king.
The white king takes the rook. Black has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate, a draw.

claims.statement: With best play the position is a draw for Black (tablebase).
After Ra7+ the position is a draw (tablebase).
Rc7 loses (tablebase).
The black king has no legal move even now.
The rook on a7 gives check to the king on a8.
After Kxa7 the black king still has no legal move.
After Kxa7 nothing attacks the black king.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the capture is forced, and afterwards your side has no legal move and is not in check. That usually needs your king boxed in, often on the edge or in a corner, and no pawn or piece able to move.
**Check:** if your side has any legal move left, there is no stalemate. Count your own legal moves after the capture.

steps.title: Same sacrifice, one change
steps.prompt: Same position, one change: Black has an extra pawn on a7. Predict, then check.

When you were losing, did you check whether giving up a piece would leave your side with no legal move? When you were winning, did you count the opponent's legal moves before each quiet move? Where did you nearly stalemate a won position, or miss a draw?

title: Stalemate in mixed endings: save the draw, avoid the trap
outcomes: Finds the stalemate resource for the losing side when the theme is not named
Avoids the quiet move that stalemates when ahead
Counts the opponent's legal moves after a candidate move before playing it
Recognises an ending where stalemate cannot arise

steps.text:
In *Stalemate as a rescue* you were told to look for the stalemate. Now the theme is not named and either side may need the idea.
**Behind:** can I give up a piece so that, after it is taken, I have no legal move and am not in check?
**Ahead:** does my quiet move leave the opponent with no legal move?
Both are one count of the legal moves of the side that would be left to move.

steps.caption: White to move. Two quiet queen moves would stalemate Black.

line.say: Checkmate: the king on g6 covers g7 and h7, and the queen covers the back rank.

claims.statement: Qd8 is checkmate.
Qh6 would be a stalemate: the tablebase gives a draw.
Qf6 would be a stalemate: the tablebase gives a draw.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the opponent has to take the piece (a check forces it) or has nothing better, and afterwards the side to move has no legal move with any piece and is not in check. **Rule of thumb:** it happens mostly with a king on the edge or in a corner.
**Test before every quiet move:** one black pawn or piece that can still move ends the stalemate, for the trick and for the trap.

steps.title: The same queen move, one spare move
steps.prompt: Predict first: a black pawn stands on a7 in the second position.
In the last positions, did you count the opponent's legal moves before you moved, or after you saw the board?

title: Stalemate conditions: spare moves and the promoted piece
outcomes: Predicts whether a stalemate still arises after one change to the position
Says how a spare pawn move removes a stalemate and how a blocked pawn does not
Chooses the promoted piece that avoids the stalemate
Recognises a king with room to move, where stalemate cannot arise

steps.text:
You can already find a stalemate (*Stalemate as a rescue*, *Stalemate in mixed endings: save the draw, avoid the trap*). Now you predict what one change does. Three conditions decide it:
**Spare moves:** any pawn or piece that can move.
**The promoted piece:** a queen can stalemate where a rook still wins.
**A pawn that cannot move** gives no spare move.

steps.caption: White promotes on f8. The piece chosen decides the result.

line.say: The rook leaves the g7 square free, so Black is not stalemated.
The black king moves and attacks the rook.
The rook steps away; king and rook win against a lone king.

claims.statement: After f8=R White wins (tablebase).
After f8=Q the game is drawn, by stalemate (tablebase).
After f8=Q the black king has no legal move.

steps.text:
**When a stalemate holds:** the side to move has no legal move with any piece and is not in check. **Rule of thumb:** a king on the edge, with no other black piece able to move.
**When it fails:** a pawn or piece that can move; a different promoted piece; a king with room. Before you rely on a stalemate, list every legal move of the side to move.

steps.title: Same queen move, one spare move
steps.prompt: Predict first: in the second position the black pawn is on h7, where it can move.
Which condition did you check first: the spare moves, the promoted piece or the pawn that could not move? Which did you forget?

title: Trapped pieces, and pieces that are only cut off
outcomes: Counts the escape squares of an attacked piece and says which are covered
Wins a trapped piece by attacking it
Tells a trapped piece from one that is only cut off

steps.text:
A piece is **trapped** when it is attacked, or can be attacked, and every square it can go to loses it. Knights on the rim and bishops that grabbed a pawn are the usual victims.
To trap a piece, count its escape squares and ask which of them you cover.

steps.caption: White to move. The black knight stands on the rim.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight. Its squares b3 and c4 are covered and b7 and c6 are taken.
Black makes some other move.
The pawn takes the knight.

claims.statement: b4 wins the knight along the engine line.

steps.text:
Trapped is not the same as cut off. A piece that is **cut off** from the action still has a safe square, so you cannot win it. Before you attack, ask:
**Which squares can it reach?**
**Which of them do I cover?**
**Can it capture something, or can its friends help?**

steps.title: Trapped or only cut off?
steps.prompt: In the second position the white pawn stands on d2, not d3.
When you counted escape squares, did you check each one for a defender or a counter-attack, or only whether it was empty?

title: Trapped, or only cut off? Count the ways out
outcomes: Finds the piece that can be won by trapping in a mixed set
Counts every way out before calling a piece trapped: retreat, capture, counter-threat
Tells a piece that is cut off but can retreat from a piece that is lost
Recognises a piece shut in by its own pawns that nothing attacks

steps.text:
In *Trapped pieces, and pieces that are only cut off* you counted escape squares. Now count **every way out**:
**A retreat square** that is safe.
**Capturing** the attacker or a guard.
**A counter-threat** that the opponent must answer.
If none works, the piece is lost. The same count tells you when your own piece is in danger.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white knight on g4 has few squares.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight. Along the engine line it wins a piece.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is h5 (depth 16).
Along the engine's best-defence line h5 nets Black at least a minor piece.

steps.text:
**When it works:** every square the piece can reach is covered or occupied, and no capture or counter-threat frees it. **Rule of thumb:** a piece with no safe move is usually lost.
**When it fails:** one safe retreat, or a way to capture a guard. A bishop shut in by its own pawns is not trapped if nothing attacks it. Count the ways out of the piece, then attack.

steps.title: Same bishop, one blocked square
steps.prompt: Predict first: in the second position the white king stands on c2, not b2.
When you called a piece trapped, had you counted retreat squares, captures and counter-threats, or only the retreat squares?

title: Underpromotion: when a knight or rook beats the queen
outcomes: Finds the promotion to a knight that gives check and attacks a second piece
Chooses a rook or a knight where a queen would stalemate
Checks the queen promotion first and says why it fails
Says when the queen is simply right

steps.text: When a pawn reaches the last rank, you choose its new piece. The queen is the usual choice because it is strongest. Sometimes another piece is better. A **knight** can give check and attack a second piece at once. A **rook** can win where a queen would leave the opponent with no legal move and no check: **stalemate**, a draw. Choosing a weaker piece on purpose is **underpromotion**.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has a queen on d7; the pawn on b7 is about to promote.

line.say: Underpromotion: a knight. It gives check to the king on a6 and attacks the queen on d7.
The king must move. Nothing can capture the knight on b8.
The knight takes the queen. The tablebase says White wins this position.

claims.statement: b8=N is legal.
A knight on b8 attacks a6 (the king) and d7 (the queen).
No black piece can capture a knight on b8, so the king must move.
White wins this position (tablebase).
Promoting to a knight keeps the win (tablebase).
Promoting to a queen loses (tablebase).

steps.text:
Check the queen first. Ask two questions.
**Does the queen promotion fail?** It might stalemate, or a knight's check and fork might win more.
**Does a knight on that square give check and attack a second piece?** As with any fork, ask whether the knight can be captured and whether the second target is worth taking.
*Rule of thumb:* the queen is the default. These questions find the exceptions.

steps.title: Does the knight still fork?
steps.prompt: In the second position Black's rook has moved from d7 to b7. In the third, no pawn can promote. Predict, then check.
Which part is least clear: seeing the knight fork, seeing the stalemate, or deciding that the queen is simply right?

title: Underpromotion: choose among four pieces
outcomes: Checks each of the four promotions instead of choosing by habit
Chooses the promoted piece that wins in a mixed set of endings
Says when the queen is the right choice, including when another piece wins as well

steps.text:
This lesson follows **Underpromotion: when a knight or rook beats the queen**. There you were told to underpromote. Now the position does not say, and the queen is often right.
For each of the four pieces ask: does the enemy king have a legal move (a queen can stalemate)? Does the piece give a check or fork that wins? Can it be captured, and does the win survive?

**The queen is correct** when it wins and the other pieces draw, or when another piece wins as well and adds nothing. **Another piece is correct** when the queen stalemates or loses to a reply it avoids.
In the next three positions only the promotion changes the result. The items state what was checked in the small endings.

steps.prompt: White to move in each position. Choose the promotion that wins. One change each time.
Name one promotion you rejected without checking in the silent positions. What would you have to ask to reject it properly: king moves, check, capture?

title: X-ray and batteries: the piece behind joins in
outcomes: Counts attackers and defenders of a square including the pieces behind
Finds the capture sequence in which the rear piece joins in
Checks that the front piece is free to capture before counting on the battery
Tells a battery from a lone piece with nothing behind it

steps.text:
Two of your pieces on one line form a **battery**. The rear piece attacks, or defends, *through* the front one: once the front piece captures or moves away, the rear piece joins in. This is called an **x-ray**.
When you count attackers and defenders, include the pieces behind. Two rooks on a file are two attackers, not one.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop on b1 stands behind the queen on d3, on the same diagonal as h7.

line.say: Qxh7 is checkmate. The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop behind it guards h7.

claims.statement: Qxh7 is checkmate.
Only the king attacks h7.
Before the capture the bishop does not reach h7: the queen is in the way.
After the queen has gone to h7, the bishop guards it.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the front piece can capture and leave the line, and the piece behind moves along that line. **Rule of thumb:** count attackers and defenders including the pieces behind, cheapest capture first, and remember that either side may stop trading.
**When it fails:** the front piece is pinned and cannot capture, or nothing stands behind it, so there is only one attacker.

steps.title: Same battery, one change
steps.prompt: Same position, one change: a black bishop stands on b5 instead of b7. Predict, then check.
In the silent positions, how many attackers and how many defenders did you count on the key square, including the pieces behind? Did you check whether the front piece was free to capture?

title: X-ray: count every piece on the line
outcomes: Counts the attackers and the defenders of a square, including the pieces behind others
Plays out the exchange in order of counting value and says who comes out ahead
Finds the winning capture sequence in a mixed position

steps.text:
This lesson follows **X-ray and batteries: the piece behind joins in**. There you were told that an x-ray existed. Now you count it yourself.
On the square in question list your attackers, including each piece standing behind another on the same line, and then the defenders. Play the exchange with the cheapest piece first. Either side may stop, so ask who runs out of pieces first.

**The count works** when the rear piece stands on the same line and the front piece will leave by capture or by moving. **It fails** when the front piece cannot capture, or when a second defender arrives. **Rule of thumb:** counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 only guide the order; check the last capture, because the side that makes it must not be recaptured.

steps.title: Same exchange, one change
steps.prompt: White to move: does the first rook capture on the e-file win a rook? One change each time. Predict, then check.
Pick one silent position. Write the attackers of the key square, including the pieces behind, then the defenders, then who runs out first. Was your first count right?

title: X-ray: predict how the count changes
outcomes: Predicts how the count changes when a defender is added, the front piece is pinned or the rear piece is missing
Verifies a capture sequence square by square before playing the first capture
Says which changes to a position leave the count as it was

steps.text:
This lesson follows **X-ray and batteries: the piece behind joins in** and **X-ray: count every piece on the line**. Here the count is not given; you predict it after a change.
Start from a battery that wins. Change one thing: a defender arrives, the front piece becomes pinned, or the rear piece leaves the line. Predict whether the count still wins, then check it square by square.

**Three changes that matter:** a new defender of the target square; a front piece pinned to its king, so it cannot capture and the rear piece never joins in; a rear piece that no longer stands on the line.
**A change that does not matter:** a move that touches neither the line nor the target. **Rule of thumb:** recount after every change; never carry the old count over.

steps.title: Same battery, one change
steps.prompt: Black to move: does the first rook capture on the e-file win a rook? One change each time. Predict, then check.
Write the three changes from this lesson on paper. For one game position of your own with two rooks on a file, predict what each change would do to the count, then check one of them.

title: In-between moves: a check or capture first
outcomes: Asks, before a capture or recapture, whether a check or capture can be played first
Finds the in-between check or capture when told one exists
Re-counts the exchange to see that the original capture still wins what was expected
Recognises a position where the plain recapture is simply best

steps.text:
An **in-between move** (German: *Zwischenzug*) is a forcing move you play *before* the reply your opponent expects, such as the recapture. It is usually a **check**, which the opponent must answer, or a **capture**.
The question to ask before any capture or recapture: **is there a check or capture I can play first, and does my original capture still work afterwards?**

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4, and Black's bishop on a6 attacks the white rook on b5. The expected move is to take on d4.

line.say: The attacked rook moves with check along the c-file. Black has to answer the check first.
The king steps aside. The white rook has left b5, so the bishop can no longer take it there.
Now the pawn takes the rook on d4. Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Rc5+ (depth 16).
Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.
Taking at once with cxd4 is at least 600 centipawns worse (engine).
Black's bishop on a6 attacks the rook on b5.
The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the in-between move forces a reply, and afterwards the capture you wanted still wins what you expected. **Rule of thumb:** look at checks first, because the reply is forced.
**When it fails:** for example when a pawn defends the target, so the follow-up capture wins nothing. After the forcing move, count the exchange again, and ask whether the opponent has an in-between move of their own.

steps.title: Same exchange, one change
steps.prompt: The black rook on d8 and the white rook on d1 face each other on the d-file. In the next position a white pawn stands on f4 instead of f2. Predict, then check.

In the silent positions, what did you expect your opponent to do next, and did you check that your capture still worked after your forcing move? (The practice puzzles carry Lichess's automatic theme label, which is not always an exact fit for this lesson.)

title: In-between moves in exchanges: yours and theirs
outcomes: Finds the in-between check or capture in a mixed exchange
Re-counts an exchange after the forcing move before relying on it
Does not rely on a recapture that the opponent can sidestep with a forcing move
Recognises an exchange where the plain recapture is best

steps.text:
In *In-between moves: a check or capture first* you found the forcing move before a recapture. In exchanges both sides can play one.
**Before you rely on a recapture:** can the opponent play a check or capture first?
**Before you play your own in-between move:** after it, does the original capture still win what you expected?
Count again after every forcing move.

steps.caption: Black to move. The rooks on b7 and f7 attack each other, and the bishop on f3 defends the rook on b7. The knight on d4 attacks that bishop.

line.say: The knight takes with check, an in-between move.
Suppose White takes the knight.
Now the rook takes the rook on b7.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Nxf3+ (depth 16).
Along the engine's best-defence line Nxf3+ nets Black at least six points of material.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the forcing move leaves your original capture available and the target cannot escape with a tempo. **Rule of thumb:** look at checks first, because the reply is forced.
**When it fails:** a pawn or piece now guards the target, so the capture wins nothing, or the opponent has a forcing move of their own. Recount after the forcing move.

steps.title: Same in-between check, one new guard
steps.prompt: Predict first: in the second position a white pawn stands on b3 instead of b4.
In the exchanges where you relied on a recapture, did you ask what the opponent could play first?

title: In-between moves: recount with their check
outcomes: Lists the checks and captures of both sides before trusting an exchange count
Predicts which side gains once the best in-between move of each side has been played
Tells a position where a check changes the count from one where it does not

steps.text: This lesson follows **In-between moves: a check or capture first** and **In-between moves in exchanges: yours and theirs**. Before you trust a count such as 'I take, he takes, I take again', list the **checks and captures of both sides** at each step, then recount. The question is not only 'do I have a check?' but 'who gains once every check has been played?'

steps.caption: White to move. Both white rooks are aimed at the black rook on a1 and the bishop on g8.

line.say: Rxg8+ is check, so the rook takes the bishop with tempo.
Black takes the rook back.
Now the second rook takes the black rook: a rook and a bishop for a rook.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Rxg8+ (depth 16).
The rook on a7 attacks the black rook on a1.
Along the engine line White ends material ahead.

steps.text:
**The check pays** when your second capture is still there afterwards and the opponent has no check of their own. **Rule of thumb:** before relying on a count, list both sides' checks.
**It fails** when the target is no longer attacked, or when the opponent's check wins back enough to level the count.
Recount after every forcing move, for both sides.

steps.title: One change, and the count changes
steps.prompt: Same pieces, one change each time. Predict who gains, then check.
When you counted a capture sequence in the silent positions, did you list the opponent's checks as well as your own? Which side's checks did you forget first?
